meta.note: Hand-curated corpus. Every proverb is grouped into a concept cluster with equivalents across cultures. Only genuine, widely attested folk proverbs are included; sources cited per proverb where known, and unattributed items are folk-traditional and marked as such.

concepts.title: Hypocrisy — the accuser guilty of the same fault
concepts.gloss: One who criticises another for a fault they themselves possess.
concepts.attestation_source: Thomas Shelton, translation of Don Quixote (English form)

proverbs.original: The pot calling the kettle black.
proverbs.literal_en: The pot calling the kettle black.
proverbs.meaning_en: The accuser has the very fault they accuse another of.
proverbs.notes: First recorded in Shelton's 1620 translation of Cervantes: 'You are like what is said the frying pan said to the kettle, Avant, black brows.'

proverbs.original: Είπε ο γάιδαρος τον πετεινό κεφάλα.
proverbs.transliteration: Eípe o gáidaros ton peteinó kefála.
proverbs.literal_en: The donkey called the rooster big-headed.
proverbs.meaning_en: Same as pot/kettle — accusing another of one's own visible flaw.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; recorded across mainland Greece and the islands.

proverbs.original: Dijo la sartén al cazo: quítate allá que me tiznas.
proverbs.literal_en: The frying pan said to the pot: get away from me, you're smudging me.
proverbs.meaning_en: The one already black complains of being blackened.
proverbs.notes: The Cervantes root of the English proverb; Don Quixote II, ch. 67.

proverbs.literal_en: The camel does not see its own hump.
proverbs.meaning_en: We see the faults of others but not our own.
proverbs.notes: Widely attested across Arabic-speaking cultures; often paired with 'wa yashūf ḥardabet akhūh' — 'but sees his brother's hump.'

proverbs.literal_en: The soldier who fled fifty paces laughs at the one who fled a hundred.
proverbs.meaning_en: Both are cowards; the slightly less guilty mocks the slightly more guilty.
proverbs.notes: From Mencius (孟子·梁惠王上), 4th century BCE — one of the oldest recorded forms of this concept.

proverbs.original: Чья бы корова мычала, а твоя бы молчала.
proverbs.transliteration: Ch'ya by korova mychala, a tvoya by molchala.
proverbs.literal_en: Whoever's cow may moo, yours should keep silent.
proverbs.meaning_en: You of all people have no right to criticise.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the retort form — addressed directly to the hypocritical accuser.

proverbs.original: Tencere dibin kara. — Seninki benden kara.
proverbs.literal_en: 'Pot, your bottom is black.' — 'Yours is blacker than mine.'
proverbs.meaning_en: Two equally sooty pots accuse each other.
proverbs.notes: A dialogue proverb; the exchange itself is quoted as a unit.

proverbs.original: دیگ به دیگ می‌گوید رویت سیاه.
proverbs.transliteration: Dīg be dīg mīgūyad rūyat siyāh.
proverbs.literal_en: The pot says to the pot: your face is black.
proverbs.meaning_en: The accuser bears the same stain.
proverbs.notes: Persian keeps the cooking-pot image of the European forms; folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: सूप बोले तो बोले, छलनी क्या बोले जिसमें बहत्तर छेद।
proverbs.transliteration: Sūp bole to bole, chhalnī kyā bole jismeṉ bahattar chhed.
proverbs.literal_en: The winnowing tray may speak — but why should the sieve, which has seventy-two holes?
proverbs.meaning_en: The one riddled with faults has least standing to criticise.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the sieve's seventy-two holes are proverbially fixed.

proverbs.original: Ein Esel schimpft den anderen Langohr.
proverbs.literal_en: One donkey calls the other 'long-ears'.
proverbs.meaning_en: The accuser mocks his own most obvious trait in another.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; note the parallel with the Greek donkey-and-rooster form.

proverbs.original: C'est l'hôpital qui se moque de la charité.
proverbs.literal_en: It is the hospital mocking the charity-house.
proverbs.meaning_en: One institution of the wretched laughing at the other — pure projection.
proverbs.notes: Both were institutions for the poor and sick under the Ancien Régime.

proverbs.original: Il bue che dice cornuto all'asino.
proverbs.literal_en: The ox calling the donkey 'horned'.
proverbs.meaning_en: The horned one accuses the hornless of his own feature.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; common in the form 'il bue dice cornuto all'asino'.

proverbs.literal_en: The eye-crud laughs at the nose-crud.
proverbs.notes: Deliberately vulgar — the register is part of the point; folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: 똥 묻은 개가 겨 묻은 개 나무란다.
proverbs.transliteration: Ttong mudeun gae-ga gyeo mudeun gae namuranda.
proverbs.literal_en: The dog smeared with dung scolds the dog smeared with chaff.
proverbs.meaning_en: The one with the greater fault rebukes the one with the lesser.
proverbs.notes: One of the most widely quoted Korean proverbs; folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: O sujo falando do mal lavado.
proverbs.literal_en: The dirty one talking about the badly washed.
proverbs.meaning_en: The filthier accuses the less filthy.
proverbs.notes: Especially common in Brazilian Portuguese; folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: Przyganiał kocioł garnkowi, a sam smoli.
proverbs.literal_en: The kettle blamed the pot, though it blackens things itself.
proverbs.meaning_en: Direct Polish cousin of the pot/kettle form.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; often shortened to 'przyganiał kocioł garnkowi'.

proverbs.literal_en: Whoever disqualifies others, disqualifies by his own defect.
proverbs.meaning_en: The fault you find in others is your own.
proverbs.notes: Babylonian Talmud, Kiddushin 70a — a rabbinic formulation of the projection insight.

concepts.title: A certain good is worth more than a hoped-for greater one
concepts.gloss: Prefer the small thing you have to the large thing you might get.
concepts.attestation_source: Aesop, 'The Nightingale and the Hawk'; canonical English form 15th c.

proverbs.original: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
proverbs.literal_en: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
proverbs.meaning_en: One sure thing is better than two uncertain ones.
proverbs.notes: Recorded in English by John Capgrave, 1450.

proverbs.original: Κάλλιο πέντε και στο χέρι παρά δέκα και καρτέρει.
proverbs.transliteration: Kállio pénte kai sto chéri pará déka kai kartérei.
proverbs.literal_en: Better five in the hand than ten and wait.
proverbs.meaning_en: The certain small is better than the promised larger.
proverbs.notes: Folk proverb, widespread in modern Greek; the number pair changes regionally (five/ten, one/two).

proverbs.original: Más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando.
proverbs.literal_en: A bird in the hand is worth more than a hundred flying.
proverbs.meaning_en: The same principle, dramatised — one certain vs. a hundred uncertain.
proverbs.notes: Attested from the 16th c.; recorded by Gonzalo Correas, 1627.

proverbs.original: عصفور في اليد خير من عشرة على الشجرة.
proverbs.transliteration: ʿUṣfūr fī al-yad khayr min ʿasharat ʿalā al-shajarah.
proverbs.literal_en: A sparrow in the hand is better than ten on the tree.
proverbs.notes: Common across the Arab world; ten is the near-universal number here.

proverbs.original: 一鸟在手,胜过双鸟在林。
proverbs.transliteration: Yī niǎo zài shǒu, shèng guò shuāng niǎo zài lín.
proverbs.literal_en: One bird in the hand beats two birds in the woods.
proverbs.meaning_en: Direct calque of the European form; also expressed as 落袋为安 (luò dài wéi ān) — 'once in the pocket, then peace of mind.'
proverbs.notes: The bird form is a modern translation; the older Chinese equivalent uses the pocket/purse image.

proverbs.original: Der Spatz in der Hand ist besser als die Taube auf dem Dach.
proverbs.literal_en: The sparrow in the hand is better than the pigeon on the roof.
proverbs.meaning_en: The small certain thing beats the bigger uncertain one.
proverbs.notes: The sparrow/pigeon pair is the standard German casting of the concept.

proverbs.original: Лучше синица в руках, чем журавль в небе.
proverbs.transliteration: Luchshe sinitsa v rukakh, chem zhuravl' v nebe.
proverbs.literal_en: Better a tit in the hands than a crane in the sky.
proverbs.meaning_en: The modest bird you hold beats the grand bird you don't.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the crane is the classic Russian image of unreachable grandeur.

proverbs.original: Un tiens vaut mieux que deux tu l'auras.
proverbs.literal_en: One 'here you are' is worth more than two 'you shall have it'.
proverbs.meaning_en: A delivered promise beats two future ones.
proverbs.notes: Fixed in this form by La Fontaine, 'Le Petit Poisson et le Pêcheur' (1668).

proverbs.original: Meglio un uovo oggi che una gallina domani.
proverbs.literal_en: Better an egg today than a hen tomorrow.
proverbs.meaning_en: Today's small good beats tomorrow's promised larger one.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the egg/hen pair is the standard Italian casting.

proverbs.original: 明日の百より今日の五十。
proverbs.transliteration: Asu no hyaku yori kyō no gojū.
proverbs.literal_en: Fifty today rather than a hundred tomorrow.
proverbs.meaning_en: The certain half beats the promised whole.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; a purely numerical casting with no bird at all.

proverbs.original: Lepszy wróbel w garści niż gołąb na dachu.
proverbs.literal_en: Better a sparrow in the fist than a pigeon on the roof.
proverbs.meaning_en: Same sparrow/pigeon pair as the German form.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; shared Central European casting.

proverbs.original: Lepší vrabec v hrsti nežli holub na střeše.
proverbs.literal_en: Better a sparrow in the fist than a pigeon on the roof.
proverbs.meaning_en: The certain small over the uncertain large.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the canonical Czech form.

proverbs.original: Parempi pyy pivossa kuin kymmenen oksalla.
proverbs.literal_en: Better one grouse in the fist than ten on the branch.
proverbs.meaning_en: One bird held beats ten in the tree.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; 'pyy' is the hazel grouse, a staple of Finnish forest fowling.

proverbs.original: Bättre en fågel i handen än tio i skogen.
proverbs.literal_en: Better one bird in the hand than ten in the forest.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; Swedish raises the English 'two in the bush' to ten in the forest.

proverbs.original: Mais vale um pássaro na mão do que dois voando.
proverbs.literal_en: A bird in the hand is worth more than two flying.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; sits between the English 'two in the bush' and the Spanish 'hundred flying'.

proverbs.original: Jobb ma egy veréb, mint holnap egy túzok.
proverbs.literal_en: Better a sparrow today than a bustard tomorrow.
proverbs.meaning_en: A small bird now beats a great bird later.
proverbs.notes: The túzok (great bustard) is one of Europe's heaviest birds — the Hungarian form maximises the contrast.

concepts.title: Speech is silver; silence is gold
concepts.gloss: There is greater wisdom in holding one's tongue than in speaking.
concepts.attestation_source: Thomas Carlyle, Sartor Resartus (1836), attributing to 'Swiss inscription'; Arabic form far older.

proverbs.original: Speech is silver, silence is golden.
proverbs.literal_en: Speech is silver, silence is golden.
proverbs.meaning_en: Silence is more valuable than speech.
proverbs.notes: Popularised in English by Carlyle in 1836; the Arabic form predates it by centuries.

proverbs.literal_en: Silence is gold.
proverbs.notes: The Greeks also say: 'Κάλλιο να σε ζηλεύουνε παρά να σε λυπούνται' — better to be envied than pitied — a distant cousin.

proverbs.original: En boca cerrada no entran moscas.
proverbs.literal_en: Flies don't enter a closed mouth.
proverbs.meaning_en: Keep your mouth shut and you'll stay out of trouble.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish form emphasises the practical consequences of loose speech rather than its metaphysical value.

proverbs.original: إذا كان الكلام من فضة فالسكوت من ذهب.
proverbs.transliteration: Idhā kāna al-kalām min fiḍḍah fa-al-sukūt min dhahab.
proverbs.literal_en: If speech is of silver, then silence is of gold.
proverbs.meaning_en: Direct silver/gold contrast — the origin of the European form.
proverbs.notes: Traced to medieval Arabic wisdom literature; likely the source of Carlyle's 'Swiss inscription.'

proverbs.literal_en: Silence is gold.
proverbs.notes: Modern Chinese has adopted this direct calque; the classical form is 言多必失 (yán duō bì shī) — 'much speech necessarily fails.'

proverbs.original: Reden ist Silber, Schweigen ist Gold.
proverbs.literal_en: Talking is silver, being silent is gold.
proverbs.meaning_en: The classic silver/gold contrast in German.
proverbs.notes: The 'Swiss inscription' Carlyle cited in 1836 was in German — this exact form.

proverbs.original: La parole est d'argent, le silence est d'or.
proverbs.literal_en: Speech is of silver, silence is of gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form of the shared European/Arabic proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: The word is silver, silence is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form; proverbial since at least the 19th century.

proverbs.literal_en: If the word is silver, silence is gold.
proverbs.notes: Turkish preserves the conditional structure of the Arabic original.

proverbs.literal_en: Not saying is the flower.
proverbs.meaning_en: Some things are more beautiful left unsaid.
proverbs.notes: A distinctly Japanese casting — silence not as safety but as aesthetic perfection.

proverbs.literal_en: A fence for wisdom is silence.
proverbs.notes: Pirkei Avot 3:13 (Rabbi Akiva) — one of the oldest datable forms of the concept.

proverbs.literal_en: Speaking is silver, keeping silent is gold.
proverbs.notes: The proverb sits comfortably in a culture that famously prizes comfortable silence.

proverbs.original: Tala är silver, tiga är guld.
proverbs.literal_en: To speak is silver, to keep silent is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swedish form of the shared proverb.

concepts.title: Time heals all wounds
concepts.gloss: The passage of time softens pain and grief.
concepts.attestation_source: Menander (Greek), fragment; Latin form in Seneca.

proverbs.literal_en: Time heals all wounds.
proverbs.meaning_en: Pain fades with the passage of time.
proverbs.notes: Chaucer used a version in Troilus and Criseyde: 'as tyme hem hurt, a tyme doth hem cure.'

proverbs.literal_en: Time cures everything.
proverbs.notes: Menander (4th c. BCE) is credited with the earliest version: 'πάντων ἰατρός ἐστι τῶν ἀναγκαίων χρόνος' — 'time is the physician of all necessary things.'

proverbs.literal_en: Time cures everything.
proverbs.notes: A direct descendant of the Greek and Latin forms.

proverbs.literal_en: Time is the best cure.
proverbs.notes: A more compressed form; also common: 'مع الوقت كل جرح يندمل' — 'with time, every wound closes.'

proverbs.transliteration: Shíjiān shì zuì hǎo de liáng yào.
proverbs.literal_en: Time is the best good medicine.
proverbs.meaning_en: Time is the finest of medicines.
proverbs.notes: Modern form; classical Chinese tends to speak of 时过境迁 (shí guò jìng qiān) — 'time passes, circumstances change.'

proverbs.literal_en: Time heals all wounds.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form, descended from the Greek and Latin tradition.

proverbs.literal_en: Time cures everything.
proverbs.notes: Compressed French form of the classical proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: Time heals.
proverbs.meaning_en: The most compressed form of the concept — two words.
proverbs.notes: Everyday Russian consolation formula.

proverbs.original: Il tempo guarisce tutti i mali.
proverbs.literal_en: Time heals all ills.
proverbs.notes: Direct descendant of the Latin tradition.

proverbs.literal_en: Time is the medicine for everything.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form; medicine rather than healing is the operative image.

proverbs.literal_en: Days are medicine.
proverbs.meaning_en: The passing days themselves are the remedy.
proverbs.notes: A beloved Kansai-region expression — grief is dosed in days.

proverbs.literal_en: Time cures everything.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

concepts.title: The apple does not fall far from the tree
concepts.gloss: Children resemble their parents; qualities are inherited.
concepts.attestation_source: Recorded in 16th-c. German (Der Apfel fällt nicht weit vom Stamm); older Turkish and Welsh forms exist.

proverbs.original: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
proverbs.literal_en: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
proverbs.notes: Entered English via 19th-c. American usage, most likely borrowed from German immigrants.

proverbs.original: Το μήλο κάτω από τη μηλιά θα πέσει.
proverbs.transliteration: To mílo káto apó ti miliá tha pései.
proverbs.literal_en: The apple will fall beneath the apple tree.
proverbs.meaning_en: The offspring falls near the parent — literally and figuratively.
proverbs.notes: Also expressed: 'κατά μάνα κατά κύρη κατά γιο και θυγατέρα' — 'like the mother, like the father, like the son and daughter.'

proverbs.literal_en: From such a log, such a splinter.
proverbs.meaning_en: The splinter is the same wood as the log.
proverbs.notes: Spanish prefers the wood metaphor; the fruit-tree form is rare outside translation.

proverbs.literal_en: This cub is from that lion.
proverbs.meaning_en: The child has the character of the parent.
proverbs.notes: The image is animal rather than botanical — a lion's cub is a lion.

proverbs.transliteration: Yǒu qí fù bì yǒu qí zǐ.
proverbs.literal_en: Where there is such a father, there must be such a son.
proverbs.notes: Also: 龙生龙,凤生凤 (lóng shēng lóng, fèng shēng fèng) — 'dragons beget dragons, phoenixes beget phoenixes.'

proverbs.original: Der Apfel fällt nicht weit vom Stamm.
proverbs.literal_en: The apple does not fall far from the trunk.
proverbs.notes: The 16th-century German form is the source of the English proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: The frog's child is a frog.
proverbs.meaning_en: Offspring turn out like their parents — often used self-deprecatingly.
proverbs.notes: Unlike the neutral apple image, the Japanese form often implies ordinary parents produce ordinary children.

proverbs.literal_en: The pear falls at its own base.
proverbs.meaning_en: The fruit lands beneath its own tree.
proverbs.notes: Turkish swaps the apple for a pear; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: The apple falls not far from the apple tree.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form, cognate with the German original.

proverbs.literal_en: Such father, such son.
proverbs.notes: From the Latin 'qualis pater, talis filius'; the French prefers the direct comparison to the fruit image.

proverbs.original: De appel valt niet ver van de boom.
proverbs.literal_en: The apple does not fall far from the tree.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form, cognate with the German.

proverbs.literal_en: Not far does the apple fall from the apple tree.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: The apple does not drop far from the tree.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

proverbs.original: Äpplet faller inte långt från trädet.
proverbs.literal_en: The apple does not fall far from the tree.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swedish form.

proverbs.literal_en: The child of a fish is a little fish.
proverbs.notes: The fish image is the standard Portuguese casting; very common in Brazil.

proverbs.literal_en: Father transmits, son receives.
proverbs.meaning_en: The father's ways pass to the son.
proverbs.notes: A four-character Sino-Korean idiom (父傳子傳) in everyday proverbial use.

concepts.title: One swallow does not make a summer
concepts.gloss: A single instance is not enough to draw a general conclusion.
concepts.attestation_source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics I.7 — 'μία γὰρ χελιδὼν ἔαρ οὐ ποιεῖ.'

proverbs.original: One swallow does not make a summer.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make a summer.
proverbs.meaning_en: A single sign is insufficient evidence.
proverbs.notes: The English uses 'summer' where Aristotle used 'spring' — a translation shift dating to the 16th c.

proverbs.original: Ένα χελιδόνι δεν φέρνει την άνοιξη.
proverbs.transliteration: Éna chelidóni den férnei tin ánoixi.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not bring the spring.
proverbs.meaning_en: One instance is not enough to signal a change.
proverbs.notes: The Greek retains Aristotle's original season — spring, not summer.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make a summer.
proverbs.meaning_en: One example does not prove the rule.
proverbs.notes: Follows the English/Latin summer form.

proverbs.literal_en: One flower does not make the spring.
proverbs.meaning_en: A single sign does not prove the season has turned.
proverbs.notes: Arabic swaps the swallow for a flower — the same logic in a different image.

proverbs.transliteration: Yī huā dú fàng bú shì chūn.
proverbs.literal_en: One flower blooming alone is not spring.
proverbs.meaning_en: One good thing alone doesn't make the whole.
proverbs.notes: Often paired with the second line 百花齐放春满园 — 'a hundred flowers blooming together fill the garden with spring.'

proverbs.original: Une hirondelle ne fait pas le printemps.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make the spring.
proverbs.meaning_en: A single sign is not proof.
proverbs.notes: French keeps Aristotle's original season — spring.

proverbs.original: Eine Schwalbe macht noch keinen Sommer.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow still makes no summer.
proverbs.notes: German follows the summer variant, like English.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make spring.
proverbs.meaning_en: One sign is not the season.
proverbs.notes: Italian keeps the original spring.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make the spring.
proverbs.notes: Russian keeps the spring variant.

proverbs.original: Uma andorinha só não faz verão.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow alone does not make a summer.
proverbs.notes: Portuguese follows the summer variant.

proverbs.original: Eén zwaluw maakt nog geen zomer.
proverbs.literal_en: One swallow still makes no summer.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: With one flower, spring does not come.
proverbs.meaning_en: A single sign does not make the season.
proverbs.notes: Turkish uses the flower image, like the Arabic form.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make the spring.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form; spring variant.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make the spring.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form; spring variant.

proverbs.literal_en: One swallow does not make a summer.
proverbs.notes: Hungarian follows the summer variant.

concepts.title: Haste makes waste
concepts.gloss: Rushing leads to mistakes; deliberate action is more efficient.
concepts.attestation_source: John Heywood, 'A Dialogue Conteinying the Nomber in Effect of All the Prouerbes in the Englishe Tongue.'

proverbs.literal_en: Haste makes waste.
proverbs.notes: Also: 'more haste, less speed' — the same wisdom in different clothes.

proverbs.literal_en: The hasty one stumbles.
proverbs.notes: Also: 'κάλλιο αργά παρά ποτέ' — better late than never — the other side of the coin.

proverbs.literal_en: Dress me slowly, I'm in a hurry.
proverbs.notes: Attributed variously to Charles III of Spain and Napoleon; the paradox is what makes it stick.

proverbs.original: في العجلة الندامة وفي التأني السلامة.
proverbs.transliteration: Fī al-ʿajalah al-nadāmah wa-fī al-taʾannī al-salāmah.
proverbs.literal_en: In haste is regret; in deliberation is safety.
proverbs.meaning_en: Rushing brings regret; patience brings safety.
proverbs.notes: The pair-clause form is characteristic of classical Arabic wisdom rhetoric.

proverbs.literal_en: Desire speed and you won't arrive.
proverbs.meaning_en: Wanting to get there fast is what stops you getting there.
proverbs.notes: From the Analects of Confucius (论语·子路), 5th c. BCE — one of the oldest recorded forms of this concept in any language.

proverbs.original: 急いては事を仕損じる。
proverbs.literal_en: Hurry, and you botch the deed.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; often paired with 急がば回れ ('when in a hurry, go the long way round').

proverbs.literal_en: The devil meddles in hurried work.
proverbs.meaning_en: Haste invites error — personified as the devil.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; one of the most-quoted Turkish proverbs.

proverbs.literal_en: Hurry, hurry has no blessing.
proverbs.notes: One of the best-known Swahili proverbs; the rhyme haraka/baraka carries it.

proverbs.literal_en: Hurry, and you'll make people laugh.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the rhyme pospeshish/nasmeshish carries it.

proverbs.literal_en: A good thing wants to take its while.
proverbs.notes: Attested in German since the 16th century.

proverbs.literal_en: Slowly comes the good.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; three words, characteristically laconic Finnish.

proverbs.literal_en: The more urgent it is, the more you should go around.
proverbs.meaning_en: When rushed, take the sure detour.
proverbs.notes: Direct Korean cousin of the Japanese 急がば回れ.

concepts.title: Empty vessels make the most noise
concepts.gloss: Those who know least talk most.
concepts.attestation_source: Attested in Middle English (Chaucer era) and in Plato's Republic in an earlier form.

proverbs.original: Empty vessels make the most noise.
proverbs.literal_en: Empty vessels make the most noise.
proverbs.notes: An empty barrel drums; a full one thuds.

proverbs.original: Το άδειο βαρέλι κάνει τον πιο πολύ θόρυβο.
proverbs.transliteration: To ádeio varéli kánei ton pio polý thóryvo.
proverbs.literal_en: The empty barrel makes the most noise.
proverbs.meaning_en: The empty one is the loud one.
proverbs.notes: The barrel is the standard vessel in the Greek form.

proverbs.literal_en: Much noise and few nuts.
proverbs.notes: Cervantes used it; also the Spanish title of Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.

proverbs.literal_en: The empty drum has the loudest voice.
proverbs.meaning_en: The empty one is the loudest.
proverbs.notes: The drum image is near-universal in Arabic-speaking cultures for this concept.

proverbs.transliteration: Bàn píng shuǐ xiǎng dīng dāng.
proverbs.literal_en: A half-full bottle of water sloshes noisily.
proverbs.meaning_en: Half-knowledge is loud; full-knowledge is quiet.
proverbs.notes: Also: 满瓶不响,半瓶叮当 — 'the full bottle doesn't sound; the half bottle rattles.' The Chinese refinement: not the empty but the half-empty is the loudest — the person with just enough learning to be dangerous.

proverbs.literal_en: The empty barrel makes the loudest sound.
proverbs.meaning_en: The one with least inside is loudest.
proverbs.notes: Same barrel image as the Greek form; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: The empty barrel rattles the loudest.
proverbs.meaning_en: The empty one makes the most noise.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Empty barrels clatter the most.
proverbs.meaning_en: The least substance, the most noise.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

proverbs.literal_en: The half-filled pitcher goes along sloshing over.
proverbs.meaning_en: Half-knowledge advertises itself; full knowledge is quiet.
proverbs.notes: From the sant-poet tradition associated with Kabir; like the Chinese form, it is the half-full — not the empty — vessel that makes the noise.

concepts.title: Many hands make light work
concepts.gloss: A shared task is an easier task.
concepts.attestation_source: John Bromyard, Summa Praedicantium (14th c.); older Latin roots.

proverbs.literal_en: Many hands make light work.
proverbs.meaning_en: Shared work is lighter for everyone.
proverbs.notes: The counter-proverb — 'too many cooks spoil the broth' — cautions the opposite; English keeps both.

proverbs.original: Ένα χέρι νίβει τ' άλλο και τα δυο το πρόσωπο.
proverbs.transliteration: Éna chéri nívei t' állo kai ta dyo to prósopo.
proverbs.literal_en: One hand washes the other, and the two together wash the face.
proverbs.meaning_en: Cooperation completes the task neither could alone.
proverbs.notes: Directly descended from the ancient Greek 'χεὶρ χεῖρα νίπτει'; used by Seneca in Latin as 'manus manum lavat.'

proverbs.literal_en: Union makes strength.
proverbs.notes: Motto of Belgium and Bulgaria; used across the Spanish-speaking world in the same collective sense.

proverbs.literal_en: The hand of God is with the group.
proverbs.meaning_en: Divine favour is on the side of the collective.
proverbs.notes: Attributed to a Prophetic hadith; carries strong communal-obligation weight.

proverbs.transliteration: Zhòng rén shí chái huǒ yàn gāo.
proverbs.literal_en: When many people gather firewood, the flames rise high.
proverbs.meaning_en: Everyone contributing makes the effort large.
proverbs.notes: The firewood image is common across East Asian versions; also compare 人多力量大 (rén duō lì liàng dà) — 'many people, great strength.'

proverbs.literal_en: One hand does not clap.
proverbs.notes: Pan-Arab; the clapping image recurs across the whole Islamic cultural sphere.

proverbs.literal_en: One hand has no sound.
proverbs.meaning_en: Cooperation is the condition of accomplishment.
proverbs.notes: The Persian twin of the Arabic clapping proverb.

proverbs.original: Bir elin nesi var, iki elin sesi var.
proverbs.literal_en: What does one hand have? Two hands have a sound.
proverbs.meaning_en: Only joined hands make a sound — only joined people make a difference.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish member of the one-hand-cannot-clap family, cast as a rhyming question and answer.

proverbs.literal_en: A single palm can hardly make a sound.
proverbs.notes: Classical chengyu, rooted in a line of Han Feizi (3rd c. BCE).

proverbs.original: Umoja ni nguvu, utengano ni udhaifu.
proverbs.literal_en: Unity is strength, division is weakness.
proverbs.notes: Widely quoted across East Africa; often shortened to 'umoja ni nguvu'.

proverbs.literal_en: One man in the field is no warrior.
proverbs.meaning_en: Alone you cannot win the battle.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the negative casting of the cooperation concept.

proverbs.literal_en: Even a sheet of paper is lighter when lifted together.
proverbs.meaning_en: No task is too small to share.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the deliberately trivial object makes the point universal.

proverbs.original: Ar scáth a chéile a mhaireann na daoine.
proverbs.literal_en: In the shelter of each other, the people live.
proverbs.meaning_en: Human life depends on mutual shelter.
proverbs.notes: One of the most beloved Irish-language proverbs; 'scáth' means both shadow and shelter.

proverbs.original: Viele Hände machen schnell ein Ende.
proverbs.literal_en: Many hands quickly make an end.
proverbs.notes: Rhyming German twin of the English 'many hands make light work'.

concepts.title: Actions speak louder than words
concepts.gloss: What people do matters more than what they say.
concepts.attestation_source: John Pym, 'a word spoken in season is like an Apple of gold... but Actions are more significant'; also proverbial in classical Chinese far earlier.

proverbs.literal_en: Actions speak louder than words.
proverbs.meaning_en: Deeds carry more weight than declarations.
proverbs.notes: Widely recorded from the 17th century onward.

proverbs.literal_en: Deeds, not words.
proverbs.notes: The compressed form; also the phrase 'λόγια του αέρα' — 'words of the wind' — for empty talk.

proverbs.original: Obras son amores y no buenas razones.
proverbs.literal_en: Works are love, not fine reasons.
proverbs.meaning_en: Real love is shown by acts, not arguments.
proverbs.notes: A near-idiomatic form; the underlying ethic is identical.

proverbs.literal_en: Deeds are more eloquent than words.
proverbs.notes: Uses the rhetorical term 'ablagh' — a higher form of eloquence — for actions themselves.

proverbs.transliteration: Guāng shuō bù zuò jiǎ bǎ shì.
proverbs.literal_en: Talking without doing is fake skill.
proverbs.notes: Also: 事实胜于雄辩 (shì shí shèng yú xióng biàn) — 'facts triumph over eloquence.'

proverbs.literal_en: No words — execution.
proverbs.notes: Four-character idiom; a prized personal virtue in Japanese work culture.

proverbs.literal_en: Fewer words, more deed.
proverbs.notes: Everyday Russian exhortation, proverbial in form.

proverbs.original: C'est au pied du mur qu'on voit le maçon.
proverbs.literal_en: It is at the foot of the wall that you see the mason.
proverbs.meaning_en: Real skill shows only in the doing.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the wall is the test that talk cannot pass.

proverbs.literal_en: A person's mirror is their work — words are not looked at.
proverbs.meaning_en: Judge people by their deeds, not their talk.
proverbs.notes: A line of the Ottoman poet Ziya Pasha (19th c.) that entered everyday proverbial use.

proverbs.literal_en: Deeds say more than words.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form of the shared European proverb.

concepts.title: The grass is always greener on the other side
concepts.gloss: What we don't have looks better than what we do.
concepts.attestation_source: Ovid, Ars Amatoria: 'fertilior seges est alienis semper in agris' — 'the crop is always more fertile in another's field.'

proverbs.original: The grass is always greener on the other side of the fence.
proverbs.literal_en: The grass is always greener on the other side of the fence.
proverbs.meaning_en: What belongs to another looks better than what we have.
proverbs.notes: The modern 'other side of the fence' form is 20th-century American; the underlying image goes back to Ovid.

proverbs.original: Το ξένο ψωμί έχει εφτά κόρες.
proverbs.transliteration: To xéno psomí échei eftá kóres.
proverbs.literal_en: Someone else's bread has seven crusts.
proverbs.meaning_en: The food at another's table always seems richer.
proverbs.notes: 'Seven' as an intensifier is characteristic of Greek folk proverbs.

proverbs.original: La gallina del vecino pone huevos más grandes.
proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's chicken lays bigger eggs.
proverbs.meaning_en: What belongs to another always seems better.
proverbs.notes: Also common: 'nadie sabe lo que tiene hasta que lo pierde' — no one knows what they have until they lose it — the other half of this insight.

proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's chicken is a goose.
proverbs.meaning_en: Your neighbour's ordinary is your extraordinary.
proverbs.notes: The chicken/goose upgrade is a widespread Levantine formulation.

proverbs.transliteration: Zhè shān wàng zhe nà shān gāo.
proverbs.literal_en: Standing on this mountain, the other mountain looks taller.
proverbs.meaning_en: From wherever you stand, another place looks better.
proverbs.notes: The mountain image gives the Chinese form a particular geographic scale.

proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's hen is a goose.
proverbs.notes: The Persian twin of the Arabic chicken/goose form.

proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's chicken looks like a goose to the neighbour.
proverbs.meaning_en: Others' possessions look grander than they are.
proverbs.notes: Same chicken/goose upgrade as the Arabic and Persian; a shared regional image.

proverbs.literal_en: It is good there — where we are not.
proverbs.meaning_en: The better place is always the one you're absent from.
proverbs.notes: The bleakest and most abstract casting of the concept; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's cherries are always sweeter.
proverbs.meaning_en: What belongs to another tastes better.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the orchard variant of the concept.

proverbs.original: दूर के ढोल सुहावने लगते हैं।
proverbs.transliteration: Dūr ke ḍhol suhāvane lagte haiṉ.
proverbs.literal_en: Distant drums sound sweet.
proverbs.meaning_en: Things far away seem more attractive than they are.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the acoustic casting — distance flatters.

proverbs.original: 隣の芝生は青く見える。
proverbs.transliteration: Tonari no shibafu wa aoku mieru.
proverbs.literal_en: The neighbour's lawn looks green.
proverbs.notes: The standard modern Japanese form; a naturalised borrowing of the English lawn image.

concepts.title: Don't judge a book by its cover
concepts.gloss: External appearance does not reveal internal worth.
concepts.attestation_source: George Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (an earlier form); the phrase in current shape is late-19th-c.

proverbs.original: Don't judge a book by its cover.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't judge a book by its cover.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't judge based on outward appearance.
proverbs.notes: The book/cover metaphor is specifically English; other cultures use different images.

proverbs.original: Τα ράσα δεν κάνουν τον παπά.
proverbs.transliteration: Ta rása den kánoun ton papá.
proverbs.literal_en: The robes do not make the priest.
proverbs.notes: A direct calque of the Latin 'cucullus non facit monachum' — the hood doesn't make the monk.

proverbs.original: El hábito no hace al monje.
proverbs.literal_en: The habit does not make the monk.
proverbs.meaning_en: The uniform doesn't create the person.
proverbs.notes: Also from the Latin; the standard Spanish form.

proverbs.original: لا تحكم على الكتاب من غلافه.
proverbs.transliteration: Lā taḥkum ʿalā al-kitāb min ghilāfihi.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't judge the book by its cover.
proverbs.notes: A modern calque of the English; the older Arabic form uses the image of judging a person by their dress or by first sight.

proverbs.original: 人不可貌相,海水不可斗量。
proverbs.transliteration: Rén bù kě mào xiàng, hǎi shuǐ bù kě dǒu liáng.
proverbs.literal_en: A person cannot be judged by appearance; the sea cannot be measured by the bushel.
proverbs.meaning_en: Some things exceed the tools we use to measure them.
proverbs.notes: The paired image — person/appearance, sea/bushel — is a signature of classical Chinese proverb form.

proverbs.original: L'habit ne fait pas le moine.
proverbs.literal_en: The habit does not make the monk.
proverbs.notes: From the medieval Latin 'cucullus non facit monachum' — the root of the Greek, Spanish and Italian forms too.

proverbs.literal_en: The habit does not make the monk.
proverbs.meaning_en: Appearance does not make the person.
proverbs.notes: Italian branch of the same Latin root.

proverbs.original: Встречают по одёжке, провожают по уму.
proverbs.transliteration: Vstrechayut po odyozhke, provozhayut po umu.
proverbs.literal_en: They greet you by your clothes and see you off by your mind.
proverbs.meaning_en: First impressions go to appearance; lasting judgement goes to substance.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; unusually, it concedes that appearance does count — at first.

proverbs.original: 人は見かけによらぬもの。
proverbs.transliteration: Hito wa mikake ni yoranu mono.
proverbs.literal_en: People are not according to their appearance.
proverbs.meaning_en: You cannot read a person from the outside.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: The appearance deceives.
proverbs.notes: Maximally compressed German form — two words.

proverbs.literal_en: Not everything round is a walnut.
proverbs.notes: Built on the pun gerd (round) / gerdu (walnut); folk-traditional.

concepts.title: The love of money is the root of all evil
concepts.gloss: Greed is the source of moral corruption.
concepts.attestation_source: 1 Timothy 6:10 (New Testament); older Greek and Egyptian wisdom traditions carry the same idea.

proverbs.original: The love of money is the root of all evil.
proverbs.literal_en: The love of money is the root of all evil.
proverbs.meaning_en: It is the love of money — not money itself — that corrupts.
proverbs.notes: Frequently misquoted as 'money is the root of all evil'; the original biblical form specifies the love of money.

proverbs.original: Ρίζα πάντων των κακών εστίν η φιλαργυρία.
proverbs.transliteration: Ríza pántōn tōn kakōn estín i philargyría.
proverbs.literal_en: The love of silver is the root of all evils.
proverbs.meaning_en: Greed is the root of every evil.
proverbs.notes: The original Greek of 1 Timothy 6:10 — the source text of the English proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: A mighty gentleman is Sir Money.
proverbs.meaning_en: Money is a powerful lord — flatteringly and dangerously.
proverbs.notes: From Francisco de Quevedo's 1651 poem; the Spanish tradition personifies money more than it moralises against it.

proverbs.literal_en: Money corrupts character.
proverbs.notes: A general folk form; classical Arabic literature has many variations on the theme.

proverbs.transliteration: Yǒu qián néng shǐ guǐ tuī mò.
proverbs.literal_en: With money, you can make ghosts push the mill.
proverbs.meaning_en: Money can make even ghosts do your labour.
proverbs.notes: The Chinese observes money's power more than it condemns it — a characteristic pragmatism.

proverbs.transliteration: Jigoku no sata mo kane shidai.
proverbs.literal_en: Even the judgments of hell depend on money.
proverbs.meaning_en: Money reaches even where justice should be absolute.
proverbs.notes: Edo-period proverb; the darkest of the money proverbs — bribery works in hell itself.

proverbs.literal_en: Happiness is not in money.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; famously extended ironically — '…а в их количестве' ('…but in their quantity').

proverbs.literal_en: Money rules the world.
proverbs.notes: Attested in German since the 17th century.

proverbs.original: L'argent ne fait pas le bonheur.
proverbs.literal_en: Money does not make happiness.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; often extended ironically — 'mais il y contribue' ('but it helps').

proverbs.literal_en: And money answers everything.
proverbs.meaning_en: Money is the answer to all practical things — said with Ecclesiastes' dry irony.
proverbs.notes: Ecclesiastes 10:19; quoted proverbially in Hebrew to this day.

concepts.title: When in Rome, do as the Romans do
concepts.gloss: Adapt your behaviour to the customs of the place you are in.
concepts.attestation_source: Advice of St Ambrose to St Augustine ('si fueris Romae, Romano vivito more'), reported by Jeremy Taylor 1660.

proverbs.original: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
proverbs.literal_en: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
proverbs.meaning_en: Follow local custom wherever you are.
proverbs.notes: From St Ambrose's 4th-century advice about fasting on different days in Rome and Milan.

proverbs.original: Paese che vai, usanza che trovi.
proverbs.literal_en: Whatever country you go to, whatever custom you find.
proverbs.meaning_en: Each place has its own ways — take them as given.
proverbs.notes: The native Italian form does not mention Rome at all.

proverbs.original: A donde fueres, haz lo que vieres.
proverbs.literal_en: Wherever you go, do what you see.
proverbs.notes: Uses the old future subjunctive — the archaic grammar marks it as genuinely old.

proverbs.original: Il faut hurler avec les loups.
proverbs.literal_en: One must howl with the wolves.
proverbs.meaning_en: Blend in with those around you — sometimes with a cynical edge.
proverbs.notes: Harsher than the Roman form: conformity as survival among wolves.

proverbs.literal_en: Other countries, other customs.
proverbs.meaning_en: Customs differ; accept the local ones.
proverbs.notes: Descriptive rather than imperative — the German states the fact and leaves the conclusion to you.

proverbs.original: В чужой монастырь со своим уставом не ходят.
proverbs.transliteration: V chuzhoy monastyr' so svoim ustavom ne khodyat.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not go into another's monastery with one's own rule-book.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't impose your rules in someone else's house.
proverbs.notes: The 'ustav' is a monastic rule — the image is of a monk arriving with his own liturgical regulations.

proverbs.literal_en: Entering a village, follow its customs.
proverbs.meaning_en: Adapt to the ways of wherever you arrive.
proverbs.notes: Four-character idiom with roots in Chan Buddhist texts (Wudeng Huiyuan).

proverbs.original: 郷に入っては郷に従え。
proverbs.transliteration: Gō ni itte wa gō ni shitagae.
proverbs.literal_en: Entering the village, obey the village.
proverbs.meaning_en: Follow the customs of the place you are in.
proverbs.notes: The Japanese sibling of the Chinese form; a staple of etiquette teaching.

proverbs.literal_en: If you go to Rome, follow Roman law.
proverbs.notes: A naturalised borrowing of the European proverb, now entirely standard in Korean.

concepts.title: Strike while the iron is hot
concepts.gloss: Act at the moment of opportunity, before it cools.
concepts.attestation_source: Chaucer, Tale of Melibee — 'whil that iren is hoot, men sholden smyte'; the smithing image is far older.

proverbs.original: Strike while the iron is hot.
proverbs.literal_en: Strike while the iron is hot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Seize the moment while conditions allow.
proverbs.notes: English also says 'make hay while the sun shines' — the agricultural twin of the smithing image.

proverbs.literal_en: Iron welds at the boil.
proverbs.meaning_en: Only at peak heat — peak opportunity — does the join take.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; from forge-welding, where two pieces join only at white heat.

proverbs.original: Il faut battre le fer pendant qu'il est chaud.
proverbs.literal_en: One must beat the iron while it is hot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Act while the opportunity is live.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form of the shared European smithing proverb.

proverbs.original: Man muss das Eisen schmieden, solange es heiß ist.
proverbs.literal_en: One must forge the iron while it is hot.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.original: Al hierro caliente, batir de repente.
proverbs.literal_en: Hot iron — beat it at once.
proverbs.meaning_en: Strike immediately while conditions are right.
proverbs.notes: Recorded by Gonzalo Correas (1627); the rhyme caliente/repente carries it.

proverbs.original: Battere il ferro finché è caldo.
proverbs.literal_en: Beat the iron while it is hot.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Forge the iron while it is hot.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Iron is hammered at its right heat.
proverbs.meaning_en: Everything has its moment of workability.
proverbs.notes: 'Tav' is the smith's term for the exact working temperature — the proverb hinges on craft vocabulary.

proverbs.literal_en: Forge the iron while it is hot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Act at the moment of opportunity.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: Men moet het ijzer smeden als het heet is.
proverbs.literal_en: One must forge the iron when it is hot.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.original: Man ska smida medan järnet är varmt.
proverbs.literal_en: One should forge while the iron is warm.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swedish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Hammer while the iron is hot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Act at the moment of opportunity.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Strike the iron while it's hot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Press on while momentum is with you.
proverbs.notes: Common in both the timing sense and a momentum sense — keep going while things are moving.

proverbs.original: น้ำขึ้นให้รีบตัก
proverbs.literal_en: When the water rises, hurry to scoop it.
proverbs.meaning_en: Take your chance while it is offered.
proverbs.notes: Thai swaps the forge for the flood — opportunity as the rising water that will recede.

concepts.title: The early bird catches the worm
concepts.gloss: Advantage belongs to those who rise and act early.
concepts.attestation_source: William Camden, Remaines of a Greater Worke Concerning Britaine — 'the early bird catcheth the worme.'

proverbs.original: The early bird catches the worm.
proverbs.literal_en: The early bird catches the worm.
proverbs.meaning_en: First to act, first to gain.
proverbs.notes: Recorded by Camden in 1605.

proverbs.literal_en: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
proverbs.meaning_en: The early hours are the profitable ones.
proverbs.notes: From the Latin 'aurora habet aurum in ore'; the German rhyme Stund/Mund made it universal.

proverbs.original: A quien madruga, Dios le ayuda.
proverbs.literal_en: God helps the one who rises at dawn.
proverbs.meaning_en: Early rising attracts fortune — framed as divine favour.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; famously countered by 'no por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano' — dawn comes no earlier for all your early rising.

proverbs.literal_en: Who sleeps catches no fish.
proverbs.notes: The Italian casts it negatively — the sleeper, not the riser, is the subject.

proverbs.original: Кто рано встаёт, тому Бог подаёт.
proverbs.transliteration: Kto rano vstayot, tomu Bog podayot.
proverbs.literal_en: Who rises early, to him God gives.
proverbs.notes: The Russian twin of the Spanish form — both route the reward through God.

proverbs.literal_en: Early rising is a profit of three mon.
proverbs.meaning_en: Rising early always pays — if only a little.
proverbs.notes: The mon was a small Edo-period coin; the modesty of the sum is the charm of the proverb.

proverbs.original: Le monde appartient à ceux qui se lèvent tôt.
proverbs.literal_en: The world belongs to those who rise early.
proverbs.notes: Proverbial in French since the 18th century.

proverbs.original: Kto rano wstaje, temu Pan Bóg daje.
proverbs.literal_en: Who rises early, to him the Lord God gives.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form, rhymed wstaje/daje.

proverbs.original: De morgenstond heeft goud in de mond.
proverbs.literal_en: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
proverbs.meaning_en: The early hours are the profitable ones.
proverbs.notes: Dutch twin of the German form, from the same Latin root.

proverbs.literal_en: The morning hour has gold in its mouth.
proverbs.meaning_en: The early hours are the profitable ones.
proverbs.notes: Swedish keeps the archaic 'mund' for the sake of the old rhyme.

proverbs.literal_en: The morning birdie hops farther.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; rhymed ptáče/doskáče.

proverbs.literal_en: Who rises early finds gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Hungarian form, rhymed kel/lel.

proverbs.original: Cine se scoală de dimineață departe ajunge.
proverbs.literal_en: Who gets up in the morning reaches far.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The one who rises early covers distance.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; framed in the vocabulary of the road.

proverbs.literal_en: God helps the one who rises early.
proverbs.notes: Portuguese twin of the Spanish form, rhymed ajuda/madruga.

concepts.title: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
concepts.gloss: Do not treat an expected gain as already yours.
concepts.attestation_source: Aesop, 'The Milkmaid and Her Pail'; English form in Thomas Howell's New Sonnets (c. 1570).

proverbs.original: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't bank on an outcome that hasn't happened.
proverbs.notes: From the Aesopic tale of the milkmaid who plans her riches from a pail of unspilt milk.

proverbs.original: No vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't sell the bear's skin before hunting it.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't trade in what you haven't yet won.
proverbs.notes: The bear-skin form is shared across Romance and Germanic Europe.

proverbs.original: Il ne faut pas vendre la peau de l'ours avant de l'avoir tué.
proverbs.literal_en: One must not sell the bear's skin before having killed it.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't dispose of an ungained prize.
proverbs.notes: Fixed by La Fontaine, 'L'Ours et les deux Compagnons' (1668).

proverbs.original: Man soll den Tag nicht vor dem Abend loben.
proverbs.literal_en: One should not praise the day before the evening.
proverbs.meaning_en: Judge nothing before it is finished.
proverbs.notes: The German prefers the day/evening frame to the animal images.

proverbs.literal_en: Chicks are counted in autumn.
proverbs.meaning_en: Only the survivors of the season count.
proverbs.notes: The Russian keeps the chicken image but moves the reckoning to harvest time.

proverbs.original: Non dire gatto se non ce l'hai nel sacco.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't say 'cat' until you have it in the sack.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't announce a capture before it's secure.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; famously quoted by football manager Giovanni Trapattoni.

proverbs.original: Ακόμα δεν τον είδαμε, Γιάννη τον εβγάλαμε.
proverbs.transliteration: Akóma den ton eídame, Giánni ton evgálame.
proverbs.literal_en: We haven't seen him yet, and we've already named him Yannis.
proverbs.meaning_en: Naming — claiming — what does not yet exist.
proverbs.notes: The unborn child already has a name; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't roll up your trouser-legs before you see the stream.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't prepare for a crossing you haven't reached.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the image is of wading a stream that may not even be there.

proverbs.literal_en: Counting the skins of tanuki not yet caught.
proverbs.meaning_en: Budgeting profits from an uncaught animal.
proverbs.notes: The tanuki (raccoon dog) was hunted for its pelt; 'kawazan'yō' is literally 'pelt arithmetic'.

proverbs.original: Je moet de huid niet verkopen voor de beer geschoten is.
proverbs.literal_en: You must not sell the hide before the bear is shot.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't trade in what you haven't won.
proverbs.notes: Dutch member of the European bear-skin family.

proverbs.original: Sälj inte skinnet förrän björnen är skjuten.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't sell the pelt until the bear is shot.
proverbs.notes: Swedish member of the bear-skin family.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't divide the skin while it's still on the bear.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't share out an unwon prize.
proverbs.notes: The Polish twist: the skin is being divided while the bear is still wearing it.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't lick before it drops.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't taste the prize before it falls to you.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the image is of honey or fat about to drip.

concepts.title: Still waters run deep
concepts.gloss: The quiet ones hold the most beneath the surface — depth, and sometimes danger.
concepts.attestation_source: Latin 'altissima quaeque flumina minimo sono labi' — 'the deepest rivers flow with the least sound' (Quintus Rufus tradition).

proverbs.literal_en: Still waters run deep.
proverbs.notes: In Middle English by the 15th century; the Latin form is a millennium older.

proverbs.literal_en: Still waters are deep.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: In the quiet pool, devils dwell.
proverbs.meaning_en: Beware the placid — something lives under that stillness.
proverbs.notes: The Russian form makes the hidden depth explicitly sinister.

proverbs.original: Il n'est pire eau que l'eau qui dort.
proverbs.literal_en: There is no worse water than sleeping water.
proverbs.meaning_en: The still surface is the dangerous one.
proverbs.notes: Attested in French since the Middle Ages; like the Russian, it reads stillness as threat.

proverbs.original: Del agua mansa líbreme Dios, que de la brava me libro yo.
proverbs.literal_en: From tame water may God deliver me — from the wild I'll deliver myself.
proverbs.meaning_en: Visible danger can be handled; hidden danger needs God's help.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the two-clause form is the full version.

proverbs.literal_en: Fear the quiet river.
proverbs.meaning_en: The silent one is the one to watch.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; also said of quiet people — 'σιγανό ποταμάκι' as a wary epithet.

proverbs.literal_en: Quiet water ruins the bridges.
proverbs.meaning_en: The still current does the structural damage.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the engineering image is distinctly Italian.

proverbs.literal_en: Quiet water tears the banks.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Still water grinds the banks.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form, twin of the Polish.

proverbs.literal_en: Calm waters are deep.
proverbs.meaning_en: The quiet hold the most beneath.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Still waters have deep bottoms.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.transliteration: Nō aru taka wa tsume o kakusu.
proverbs.literal_en: The skilled hawk hides its talons.
proverbs.notes: Not a water image, but the standard Japanese equivalent cited for this concept — depth deliberately hidden.

concepts.title: A friend in need is a friend indeed
concepts.gloss: True friendship is proven in hardship.
concepts.attestation_source: Ennius — 'amicus certus in re incerta cernitur', 'a sure friend is discerned in unsure times' (quoted by Cicero, De Amicitia).

proverbs.original: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
proverbs.literal_en: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
proverbs.meaning_en: The friend who stays through hardship is the real one.
proverbs.notes: In English by the 15th century; the rhyme need/indeed fixed the form.

proverbs.literal_en: The friend shows himself in need.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form, continuous with the classical sentiment in Ennius and Cicero.

proverbs.literal_en: The friend — in the time of hardship.
proverbs.meaning_en: Friendship is defined by the hard times.
proverbs.notes: The near-rhyme ṣadīq/ḍīq makes this one of the most quoted Arabic sayings on friendship.

proverbs.original: دوست آن باشد که گیرد دست دوست / در پریشان‌حالی و درماندگی.
proverbs.transliteration: Dūst ān bāshad ke gīrad dast-e dūst / dar parīshān-ḥālī o darmāndegī.
proverbs.literal_en: A friend is one who takes a friend's hand / in distress and helplessness.
proverbs.meaning_en: Friendship is the hand extended in your worst hour.
proverbs.notes: A couplet of Saadi (13th c.) so widely quoted it functions as a proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: Friends are known in misfortune.
proverbs.meaning_en: Trouble is the test of friendship.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Freunde erkennt man in der Not.
proverbs.literal_en: One recognises friends in hardship.
proverbs.meaning_en: Need reveals who your friends are.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; also proverbial as 'Freunde in der Not gehen tausend auf ein Lot'.

proverbs.literal_en: The friend becomes evident on the black day.
proverbs.meaning_en: The dark day shows you your friends.
proverbs.notes: 'Kara gün' — the black day — is the fixed Turkish expression for calamity.

proverbs.literal_en: In adversity, true feeling is seen.
proverbs.notes: Standard Chinese form of the shared concept.

proverbs.original: Chi trova un amico trova un tesoro.
proverbs.literal_en: Who finds a friend finds a treasure.
proverbs.notes: The Italian celebrates the friend rather than testing him; ultimately biblical (Sirach 6:14).

proverbs.original: En las malas se conocen los amigos.
proverbs.literal_en: In the bad times, friends are known.
proverbs.notes: Common across the Spanish-speaking world.

proverbs.original: Prawdziwych przyjaciół poznaje się w biedzie.
proverbs.literal_en: True friends are known in poverty.
proverbs.meaning_en: Hardship is the filter of friendship.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form; 'bieda' covers both poverty and trouble.

concepts.title: Too many cooks spoil the broth
concepts.gloss: Too many people directing one task ruin it.
concepts.attestation_source: English attested in the 1570s (George Gascoigne's circle); the concept is far older and worldwide.

proverbs.original: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
proverbs.literal_en: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
proverbs.notes: The standing counter-proverb to 'many hands make light work' — English keeps both.

proverbs.literal_en: Many cooks spoil the porridge.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many decision-makers ruin the dish.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; Brei (porridge) instead of broth.

proverbs.original: 船頭多くして船山に上る。
proverbs.transliteration: Sendō ōku shite fune yama ni noboru.
proverbs.literal_en: With too many boatmen, the boat climbs the mountain.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many steersmen take the vessel somewhere absurd.
proverbs.notes: The boat ascending a mountain is the classic Japanese image of committee failure.

proverbs.literal_en: If the boatmen are many, the boat goes up the mountain.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many leaders steer into absurdity.
proverbs.notes: Korean twin of the Japanese form — a shared East Asian image.

proverbs.transliteration: Sān ge héshang méi shuǐ hē.
proverbs.literal_en: Three monks have no water to drink.
proverbs.meaning_en: One monk carries water, two share it — with three, everyone shirks and no one drinks.
proverbs.notes: From a folk tale: responsibility diffuses as numbers grow.

proverbs.original: У семи нянек дитя без глазу.
proverbs.transliteration: U semi nyanek ditya bez glazu.
proverbs.literal_en: With seven nannies, the child loses an eye.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the darkest of the cluster's images.

proverbs.original: Troppi galli a cantar non fa mai giorno.
proverbs.literal_en: With too many roosters crowing, day never dawns.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many announcers, and the thing never happens.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; northern Italian in origin.

proverbs.original: Horozu çok olan köyün sabahı geç olur.
proverbs.literal_en: The village with many roosters has a late morning.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many voices delay the outcome.
proverbs.notes: Turkish twin of the Italian rooster image.

proverbs.original: Gdzie kucharek sześć, tam nie ma co jeść.
proverbs.literal_en: Where there are six cooks, there is nothing to eat.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed sześć/jeść; standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: Trop de cuisiniers gâtent la sauce.
proverbs.literal_en: Too many cooks spoil the sauce.
proverbs.notes: The French, fittingly, spoil a sauce rather than a broth.

proverbs.original: Muchas manos en un plato hacen mucho garabato.
proverbs.literal_en: Many hands in one dish make a big scrawl.
proverbs.meaning_en: Too many participants make a mess.
proverbs.notes: Especially common in Mexico; rhymed plato/garabato.

concepts.title: Walls have ears
concepts.gloss: You are never certain you are unheard — speak with care.
concepts.first_attested: ~17th century (European forms); older in Hebrew midrash
concepts.attestation_source: Midrashic Hebrew 'oznayim la-kotel' (Vayikra Rabbah); European forms proverbial by the 1600s.

proverbs.literal_en: Walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Proverbial in English since the 17th century; revived on WWII security posters.

proverbs.literal_en: The walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: 壁に耳あり障子に目あり。
proverbs.transliteration: Kabe ni mimi ari, shōji ni me ari.
proverbs.literal_en: Walls have ears, shōji have eyes.
proverbs.meaning_en: You may be heard and seen — nowhere is private.
proverbs.notes: The paper shōji screen adds eyes to the ears; the complete surveillance couplet.

proverbs.literal_en: Beyond the wall there are ears.
proverbs.meaning_en: The other side of the wall is listening.
proverbs.notes: Classical form, with roots in the Guanzi.

proverbs.literal_en: The walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Colloquial Egyptian/Levantine form ('widān' = ears).

proverbs.literal_en: Even the walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form; heavy with Soviet-era resonance.

proverbs.literal_en: The walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: The walls hear.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish walls don't merely have ears — they actively listen.

proverbs.original: دیوار موش دارد، موش هم گوش دارد.
proverbs.transliteration: Dīvār mūsh dārad, mūsh ham gūsh dārad.
proverbs.literal_en: The wall has mice, and the mice have ears.
proverbs.meaning_en: Your words travel by unseen carriers.
proverbs.notes: The rhyme mūsh/gūsh (mouse/ear) drives the Persian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The ground has ears.
proverbs.meaning_en: Even the earth listens — nothing stays secret.
proverbs.notes: Turkish extends the listening surface from the wall to the ground itself.

proverbs.original: 낮말은 새가 듣고 밤말은 쥐가 듣는다.
proverbs.transliteration: Nanmal-eun sae-ga deutgo bammal-eun jwi-ga deunneunda.
proverbs.literal_en: Day-words are heard by birds, night-words by mice.
proverbs.meaning_en: Whatever the hour, something is listening.
proverbs.notes: One of the most-cited Korean proverbs; the day/night pairing is its signature.

proverbs.literal_en: The wall has ears.
proverbs.notes: From the midrash (Vayikra Rabbah 32:2) — among the oldest datable forms of this proverb anywhere.

proverbs.literal_en: Even the walls have ears.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

concepts.title: Once bitten, twice shy
concepts.gloss: One painful experience teaches lasting — even excessive — caution.
concepts.attestation_source: English form in R. S. Surtees (1853); the scalded-cat and burnt-child forms are medieval.

proverbs.literal_en: Once bitten, twice shy.
proverbs.meaning_en: After one bad experience, you flinch at anything similar.
proverbs.notes: Also 'a burnt child dreads the fire', attested in English since 1320.

proverbs.original: 一朝被蛇咬,十年怕井绳。
proverbs.transliteration: Yī zhāo bèi shé yǎo, shí nián pà jǐng shéng.
proverbs.literal_en: Bitten by a snake one morning, afraid of the well-rope for ten years.
proverbs.meaning_en: The coiled rope forever resembles the snake.
proverbs.notes: The proportions — one morning against ten years — are the point.

proverbs.transliteration: Atsumono ni korite namasu o fuku.
proverbs.literal_en: Scalded by hot broth, one blows on cold salad.
proverbs.meaning_en: Burnt once, you take absurd precautions ever after.
proverbs.notes: From the Chu Ci (Songs of Chu, ~3rd c. BCE) — an ancient literary borrowing into Japanese.

proverbs.original: Обжёгшись на молоке, дуют на воду.
proverbs.transliteration: Obzhyogshis' na moloke, duyut na vodu.
proverbs.literal_en: Having burnt themselves on milk, they blow on water.
proverbs.meaning_en: Past pain makes even the harmless suspect.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form of the shared burnt-on-milk family.

proverbs.original: Sütten ağzı yanan yoğurdu üfleyerek yer.
proverbs.literal_en: He whose mouth was burnt by milk eats yogurt blowing on it.
proverbs.meaning_en: Once scalded, forever cautious — even with the cold.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish member of the milk family; blowing on cold yogurt is the absurdity that carries it.

proverbs.original: مارگزیده از ریسمان سیاه و سفید می‌ترسد.
proverbs.literal_en: The snake-bitten fears the black-and-white rope.
proverbs.meaning_en: Trauma sees the snake in every rope.
proverbs.notes: Persian twin of the Chinese snake/rope image; the black-and-white banding recalls a krait.

proverbs.literal_en: A burnt child shuns the fire.
proverbs.notes: Attested in German since the Middle Ages.

proverbs.original: El gato escaldado del agua fría huye.
proverbs.literal_en: The scalded cat flees even cold water.
proverbs.notes: Attested in Spanish since the 14th century (Libro de Buen Amor tradition).

proverbs.literal_en: A scalded cat fears cold water.
proverbs.notes: Attested in French since the 13th century (Roman de Renart tradition).

proverbs.original: Όποιος καεί στο χυλό, φυσάει και το γιαούρτι.
proverbs.transliteration: Ópoios kaeí sto chyló, fysáei kai to giaoúrti.
proverbs.literal_en: Who is burnt on the porridge blows even on the yogurt.
proverbs.meaning_en: Once burnt, you blow on everything.
proverbs.notes: Greek member of the same Balkan/Anatolian yogurt family as the Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: A burnt child shuns the fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swedish form, cognate with the German.

proverbs.original: Een ezel stoot zich geen tweemaal aan dezelfde steen.
proverbs.literal_en: A donkey does not bump twice against the same stone.
proverbs.meaning_en: Even a donkey learns from one knock — so should you.
proverbs.notes: The Dutch flips the register: not trauma but common sense; often used as a rebuke.

proverbs.original: दूध का जला छाछ भी फूंक फूंक कर पीता है।
proverbs.transliteration: Dūdh kā jalā chhāchh bhī phūṉk phūṉk kar pītā hai.
proverbs.literal_en: One burnt by milk drinks even buttermilk after blowing on it.
proverbs.notes: The Hindi member of the milk family, with cool buttermilk as the absurd object of caution.

proverbs.original: لا يُلدغ المؤمن من جحر واحد مرتين.
proverbs.transliteration: Lā yuldagh al-muʾmin min juḥr wāḥid marratayn.
proverbs.literal_en: The believer is not stung from the same hole twice.
proverbs.meaning_en: Learn from the first sting; there is no excuse for the second.
proverbs.notes: A hadith of the Prophet (Bukhari, Muslim) in universal proverbial use.

concepts.title: Where there's smoke, there's fire
concepts.gloss: Rumours and signs usually point to something real.
concepts.attestation_source: Medieval French and Latin collections; proverbial across Europe by the late Middle Ages.

proverbs.literal_en: Where there's smoke, there's fire.
proverbs.meaning_en: Persistent signs indicate a real cause.
proverbs.notes: Standard English form; also 'there's no smoke without fire'.

proverbs.original: Il n'y a pas de fumée sans feu.
proverbs.literal_en: There is no smoke without fire.
proverbs.notes: Attested in French since the 13th century.

proverbs.original: Cuando el río suena, agua lleva.
proverbs.literal_en: When the river makes noise, it is carrying water.
proverbs.meaning_en: If everyone is talking, something is flowing.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish swaps smoke for the sound of a swollen river; also '…piedras trae' ('it carries stones').

proverbs.original: Wo Rauch ist, ist auch Feuer.
proverbs.literal_en: Where smoke is, fire is too.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no smoke without fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Without wind, no waves rise.
proverbs.notes: The Chinese replaces fire and smoke with wind and waves.

proverbs.original: 火のない所に煙は立たぬ。
proverbs.transliteration: Hi no nai tokoro ni kemuri wa tatanu.
proverbs.literal_en: Where there is no fire, no smoke rises.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form.

proverbs.literal_en: Smoke does not come from a place without fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no smoke without fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no smoke without a roast.
proverbs.meaning_en: The signs point to something cooking.
proverbs.notes: The Italian nose follows the smoke to the kitchen, not the hearth.

proverbs.literal_en: No smoke without fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no smoke without fire.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

concepts.title: After rain comes sunshine
concepts.gloss: Hardship passes; better times follow the bad.
concepts.attestation_source: John Milton, Comus — 'a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night'; the rain/sunshine forms are folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: Every cloud has a silver lining.
proverbs.literal_en: Every cloud has a silver lining.
proverbs.notes: The image is Milton's (Comus, 1634); proverbial by the Victorian era.

proverbs.original: Après la pluie, le beau temps.
proverbs.literal_en: After the rain, fine weather.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; attested since the Middle Ages.

proverbs.literal_en: After rain comes sunshine.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: Sunshine follows rain.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: After the rain falls, the ground hardens.
proverbs.meaning_en: The storm doesn't just pass — it leaves things stronger.
proverbs.notes: Often said after a quarrel: the relationship sets firmer for having been rained on.

proverbs.literal_en: When Pi (stagnation) peaks, Tai (peace) arrives.
proverbs.meaning_en: At the extreme of misfortune, fortune turns.
proverbs.notes: Built from two hexagrams of the I Ching — decline contains the pivot to flourishing.

proverbs.literal_en: The end of the black night is white.
proverbs.notes: A line from the classical Persian poetic tradition (attributed to Nezami) in full proverbial use.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no bad without good.
proverbs.notes: The Russian mirror of 'no smoke without fire' — same syntax, opposite comfort.

proverbs.original: No hay mal que por bien no venga.
proverbs.literal_en: There is no ill that does not come for some good.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form; title of a Calderón-era comedy, already proverbial then.

proverbs.original: Non tutto il male vien per nuocere.
proverbs.literal_en: Not all evil comes to harm.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Nie ma tego złego, co by na dobre nie wyszło.
proverbs.literal_en: There is no bad thing that does not turn out for good.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: In every affair there is some good.
proverbs.meaning_en: Whatever happens carries a hidden blessing.
proverbs.notes: Turkish folk theology in proverb form — 'hayır' is providential good.

concepts.title: The last straw — the drop that overflows the cup
concepts.gloss: A final small addition that exhausts all endurance.
concepts.attestation_source: English 'the last straw that breaks the camel's back' popularised via Dickens (Dombey and Son); the Arabic camel form is traditional.

proverbs.original: The last straw breaks the camel's back.
proverbs.literal_en: The last straw breaks the camel's back.
proverbs.meaning_en: One tiny addition finally exceeds all capacity.
proverbs.notes: Earlier English had 'the last feather breaks the horse's back' (17th c.).

proverbs.literal_en: The straw that broke the camel's back.
proverbs.notes: The camel form is native to Arabic and likely the source of the English.

proverbs.original: La gota que colmó el vaso.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop that overfilled the glass.
proverbs.notes: The Romance languages prefer the drop/vessel image to the camel.

proverbs.original: La goutte d'eau qui fait déborder le vase.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop of water that makes the vase overflow.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: Der Tropfen, der das Fass zum Überlaufen bringt.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop that brings the barrel to overflowing.
proverbs.notes: German scales the vessel up to a barrel.

proverbs.original: De druppel die de emmer doet overlopen.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop that makes the bucket overflow.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form, with a bucket.

proverbs.original: La goccia che fa traboccare il vaso.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop that makes the vase overflow.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Η σταγόνα που ξεχείλισε το ποτήρι.
proverbs.transliteration: I stagóna pou xecheílise to potíri.
proverbs.literal_en: The drop that overflowed the glass.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.literal_en: The drop of water.
proverbs.meaning_en: The final small excess — the phrase alone suffices.
proverbs.notes: So proverbial in Portuguese that the drop needs no vessel.

concepts.title: Slow and steady wins the race
concepts.gloss: Unhurried persistence beats brilliant haste.
concepts.attestation_source: Aesop, 'The Tortoise and the Hare'; the English tag is from Robert Lloyd's 1762 verse retelling.

proverbs.original: Slow and steady wins the race.
proverbs.literal_en: Slow and steady wins the race.
proverbs.notes: The moral of Aesop's tortoise, fixed in this English form in the 18th century.

proverbs.literal_en: Hasten slowly.
proverbs.notes: Suetonius records it as a favourite maxim of Augustus; Latinised as 'festina lente'.

proverbs.original: Chi va piano va sano e va lontano.
proverbs.literal_en: Who goes slowly goes safely and goes far.
proverbs.meaning_en: The measured pace is the one that arrives.
proverbs.notes: The triple rhyme piano/sano/lontano makes it one of Italy's best-loved proverbs.

proverbs.original: Rien ne sert de courir, il faut partir à point.
proverbs.literal_en: Running is useless — one must set out on time.
proverbs.notes: The opening moral of La Fontaine's 'Le Lièvre et la Tortue' (1668).

proverbs.literal_en: Hurry with leisure.
proverbs.notes: The German descendant of 'festina lente', compressed to a rhyme.

proverbs.literal_en: Ride more quietly — you will get farther.
proverbs.meaning_en: The slower traveller covers more ground in the end.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; a coachman's proverb in origin.

proverbs.literal_en: If you hurry, go around.
proverbs.meaning_en: When rushed, take the longer, surer route.
proverbs.notes: Originally advice to cross Lake Biwa by the long land road rather than the risky boat.

proverbs.literal_en: Slow work yields fine craft.
proverbs.notes: An artisan's proverb; standard in Mandarin.

proverbs.literal_en: Slowly, slowly is the way to go.
proverbs.meaning_en: The steady pace is the true pace.
proverbs.notes: Ubiquitous on the Swahili coast; famously the mantra of Kilimanjaro guides.

proverbs.original: ช้า ๆ ได้พร้าเล่มงาม
proverbs.transliteration: Cháa cháa dâi phráa lêm ngaam.
proverbs.literal_en: Slowly, slowly — you get a fine machete.
proverbs.meaning_en: Careful work produces the beautiful blade.
proverbs.notes: A smithing image again — the good knife cannot be forged in a hurry.

proverbs.original: धीरे-धीरे रे मना, धीरे सब कुछ होय। माली सींचे सौ घड़ा, ऋतु आए फल होय।
proverbs.transliteration: Dhīre-dhīre re manā, dhīre sab kuchh hoy. Mālī sīṉche sau ghaṛā, r̥tu āe phal hoy.
proverbs.literal_en: Slowly, slowly, O mind — everything happens slowly. The gardener may pour a hundred pots; fruit comes only in its season.
proverbs.notes: A doha (couplet) of the sant-poet Kabir (15th c.), in universal proverbial use.

concepts.title: Blood is thicker than water
concepts.gloss: Family bonds outweigh other ties.
concepts.attestation_source: Middle High German in Heinrich der Glîchezære's Reinhart Fuchs (c. 1180).

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is thicker than water.
proverbs.notes: In English by the 17th century, from the medieval German.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is thicker than water.
proverbs.notes: The oldest attested branch — Reinhart Fuchs, c. 1180.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is denser than water.
proverbs.notes: Fully naturalised in Chinese; used especially of overseas kin and compatriots.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood does not become water.
proverbs.notes: Colloquial Levantine form; the negative casting is the signature of the eastern Mediterranean family.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood does not become water.
proverbs.notes: The Greek member of the same negative-casting family as the Arabic and Turkish.

proverbs.literal_en: Flesh does not part from the nail.
proverbs.meaning_en: Family cannot be separated — they grow from each other.
proverbs.notes: The flesh-and-fingernail image is the standard Turkish casting of inseparable kinship.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is not water.
proverbs.notes: Compressed Slavic form.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is not water.
proverbs.meaning_en: Kinship counts — also said of hot temperament.
proverbs.notes: In Polish the phrase doubles as 'passions run hot'.

proverbs.literal_en: Blood is not water.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Het bloed kruipt waar het niet gaan kan.
proverbs.literal_en: Blood creeps where it cannot walk.
proverbs.meaning_en: Family feeling finds a way through every obstacle.
proverbs.notes: The most vivid of the family — blood as a persistent, creeping force.

concepts.title: A new broom sweeps clean
concepts.gloss: Newcomers are briefly zealous — novelty itself does the work.
concepts.attestation_source: John Heywood's proverb collection (1546) — 'the grene new brome swepith cleene.'

proverbs.literal_en: A new broom sweeps clean.
proverbs.meaning_en: New people attack the job with fresh zeal — while it lasts.
