proverbs.notes: Often completed: '…but the old broom knows the corners.'

proverbs.literal_en: New brooms sweep well.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; the sceptical continuation about old brooms and corners exists here too.

proverbs.literal_en: New brooms sweep clean.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: The new broom sweeps in a new way.
proverbs.meaning_en: A new boss imposes new ways — said warily.
proverbs.notes: The Russian reads the new broom politically: new management, new rules.

proverbs.original: Καινούργιο κοσκινάκι μου, και πού να σε κρεμάσω;
proverbs.transliteration: Kainoúrgio koskináki mou, kai poú na se kremáso?
proverbs.literal_en: My new little sieve — where shall I hang you?
proverbs.meaning_en: The new acquisition is fussed over; the fuss will fade.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; said of any novelty receiving exaggerated care.

concepts.title: Barking dogs seldom bite
concepts.gloss: The loudest threateners are the least dangerous.
concepts.attestation_source: Medieval Latin 'canes timidi vehementius latrant quam mordent' tradition (after Quintus Curtius Rufus).

proverbs.literal_en: Barking dogs seldom bite.
proverbs.notes: In English collections since the 16th century.

proverbs.literal_en: Dogs that bark do not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.original: Chien qui aboie ne mord pas.
proverbs.literal_en: A dog that barks does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: A barking dog is little of a biter.
proverbs.meaning_en: The louder the bark, the weaker the bite.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed ladrador/mordedor; standard across the Spanish-speaking world.

proverbs.literal_en: The dog that barks does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The barking dog does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: A dog that barks does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.original: Не бойся собаки брехливой, бойся молчаливой.
proverbs.transliteration: Ne boysya sobaki brekhlivoy, boysya molchalivoy.
proverbs.literal_en: Fear not the yappy dog — fear the silent one.
proverbs.meaning_en: The quiet threat is the real one.
proverbs.notes: The Russian states the corollary outright: watch the one that doesn't bark.

proverbs.transliteration: Yǎo rén de gǒu bú lòu chǐ.
proverbs.literal_en: The dog that bites doesn't bare its teeth.
proverbs.notes: The Chinese, like the Russian, inverts the frame to warn of the silent biter.

proverbs.literal_en: The dog that barks does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.literal_en: The dog that barks does not bite.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

concepts.title: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth
concepts.gloss: Don't inspect or criticise what you are given for free.
concepts.attestation_source: St Jerome, Commentary on Ephesians — 'noli equi dentes inspicere donati' ('never inspect the teeth of a given horse').

proverbs.original: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't look a gift horse in the mouth.
proverbs.notes: A horse's age is read from its teeth — checking a gifted horse's mouth is pricing the gift.

proverbs.original: A caballo regalado no le mires el diente.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't look at the tooth of a gifted horse.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form of Jerome's Latin.

proverbs.original: À cheval donné on ne regarde pas les dents.
proverbs.literal_en: On a given horse one does not look at the teeth.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: Einem geschenkten Gaul schaut man nicht ins Maul.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not look into the mouth of a gifted nag.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed Gaul/Maul — the German form is the catchiest of the family.

proverbs.original: A caval donato non si guarda in bocca.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not look a gifted horse in the mouth.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Дарёному коню в зубы не смотрят.
proverbs.transliteration: Daryonomu konyu v zuby ne smotryat.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not look a gifted horse in the teeth.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Darowanemu koniowi w zęby się nie zagląda.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not peer into the teeth of a gifted horse.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: A cavalo dado não se olham os dentes.
proverbs.literal_en: On a given horse one does not look at the teeth.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.original: Een gegeven paard mag men niet in de bek kijken.
proverbs.literal_en: A given horse must not be looked at in the mouth.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.original: Calul de dar nu se caută la dinți.
proverbs.literal_en: The gift horse is not examined at the teeth.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

proverbs.original: Ajándék lónak ne nézd a fogát.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't look at the teeth of a gift horse.
proverbs.notes: Standard Hungarian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't gaze at the teeth of a gifted horse.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form.

proverbs.literal_en: One does not look into the mouth of a gift horse.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form of the pan-European proverb.

proverbs.original: Του χάριζαν γάιδαρο και τον κοίταζε στα δόντια.
proverbs.transliteration: Tou chárizan gáidaro kai ton koítaze sta dóntia.
proverbs.literal_en: They were gifting him a donkey — and he was checking its teeth.
proverbs.meaning_en: Said mockingly of one who appraises a free gift.
proverbs.notes: The Greek turns the maxim into an anecdote about a specific ingrate — with a donkey, not a horse.

concepts.title: The shoemaker's children go barefoot
concepts.gloss: Professionals neglect their own household's need of their skill.
concepts.attestation_source: John Heywood (1546) — 'who is worse shod than the shoemaker's wife?'; parallel forms are traditional worldwide.

proverbs.literal_en: The shoemaker's children go barefoot.
proverbs.meaning_en: The expert's own family goes unserved.
proverbs.notes: Heywood's 1546 version asks 'who is worse shod than the shoemaker's wife?'

proverbs.original: En casa de herrero, cuchillo de palo.
proverbs.literal_en: In the blacksmith's house, a wooden knife.
proverbs.meaning_en: The craftsman's home lacks his own craft.
proverbs.notes: The standard Spanish form moves the irony to the smithy.

proverbs.original: Casa de ferreiro, espeto de pau.
proverbs.literal_en: Blacksmith's house, wooden skewer.
proverbs.meaning_en: The craftsman's home lacks his own craft.
proverbs.notes: Portuguese twin of the Spanish smithy form.

proverbs.original: Les cordonniers sont toujours les plus mal chaussés.
proverbs.literal_en: The cobblers are always the worst shod.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; attested since Montaigne's era.

proverbs.original: Der Schuster hat die schlechtesten Schuhe.
proverbs.literal_en: The shoemaker has the worst shoes.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: The carpenter's door is falling off its hinges.
proverbs.meaning_en: The craftsman's home shows the neglect of his own craft.
proverbs.notes: Colloquial Egyptian; one of the most-quoted Egyptian proverbs.

proverbs.original: کوزه‌گر از کوزه شکسته آب می‌خورد.
proverbs.transliteration: Kūzegar az kūze-ye shekaste āb mīkhorad.
proverbs.literal_en: The potter drinks water from a broken jug.
proverbs.meaning_en: The maker keeps the worst of his own wares.
proverbs.notes: Standard Persian form; the potter's cracked jug is its fixed image.

proverbs.literal_en: The cobbler without boots.
proverbs.meaning_en: The specialist lacking his own product.
proverbs.notes: Compressed to a three-word noun phrase — usable as a label for any such case.

proverbs.literal_en: The shoemaker walks without shoes.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: The tailor cannot mend his own tear.
proverbs.meaning_en: We fail to apply our skill to ourselves.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish moves the trade to tailoring — and makes the failure an inability, not mere neglect.

concepts.title: Measure twice, cut once
concepts.gloss: Check thoroughly before taking an irreversible action.
concepts.attestation_source: Carpenter's and tailor's folk wisdom across many cultures; no single classical source.

proverbs.literal_en: Measure twice, cut once.
proverbs.meaning_en: Verify before committing; the cut cannot be undone.
proverbs.notes: Carpenter's folk wisdom; proverbial in English by the 19th century.

proverbs.original: Семь раз отмерь, один раз отрежь.
proverbs.transliteration: Sem' raz otmer', odin raz otrezh'.
proverbs.literal_en: Measure seven times, cut once.
proverbs.meaning_en: Check to excess before the irreversible act.
proverbs.notes: The Russian raises the count to seven — its usual intensifier.

proverbs.literal_en: Measure nine times, cut once.
proverbs.notes: Turkish outbids the Russian seven with nine.

proverbs.literal_en: Measure twice, cut once.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form.

proverbs.literal_en: Think three times, then act.
proverbs.notes: From the Analects (5.20) — where Confucius wryly replies that twice is enough.

proverbs.literal_en: Tap the stone bridge before crossing it.
proverbs.meaning_en: Test even the obviously solid before trusting it.
proverbs.notes: Said of the extremely cautious — sometimes admiringly, sometimes not.

proverbs.literal_en: First weigh, then dare.
proverbs.notes: The pun wägen/wagen (weigh/dare) carries it; motto of the Prussian field marshal Moltke.

concepts.title: Better late than never
concepts.gloss: A late arrival or repair still beats none at all.
concepts.attestation_source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita IV — 'potius sero quam numquam.'

proverbs.literal_en: Better late than never.
proverbs.meaning_en: Lateness is forgivable; absence is not.
proverbs.notes: Direct descendant of Livy's Latin; in English by Chaucer's time.

proverbs.literal_en: Better late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.literal_en: Better is late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: Late is worth more than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Better late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Better late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Better late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Rather late than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.original: Mai bine mai târziu decât niciodată.
proverbs.literal_en: Better later than never.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Let it be late — but let it not be hard.
proverbs.meaning_en: Delay is acceptable if it spares difficulty.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish shifts the trade-off: not late-versus-never but late-versus-painful.

proverbs.transliteration: Wáng yáng bǔ láo, wèi wéi wǎn yě.
proverbs.literal_en: Mend the pen after losing a sheep — it is not yet too late.
proverbs.meaning_en: Repair after a loss still prevents the next one.
proverbs.notes: From the Stratagems of the Warring States (Zhanguo Ce), 3rd century BCE.

concepts.title: The tongue has no bones — yet it breaks bones
concepts.gloss: Words wound more deeply and permanently than weapons.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-traditional across the Mediterranean and Middle East; the Hebrew form is biblical (Proverbs 18:21).

proverbs.original: Η γλώσσα κόκκαλα δεν έχει και κόκκαλα τσακίζει.
proverbs.transliteration: I glóssa kókkala den échei kai kókkala tsakízei.
proverbs.literal_en: The tongue has no bones, yet it shatters bones.
proverbs.meaning_en: The boneless organ does the breaking.
proverbs.notes: The canonical Greek form of the concept, built on the bone paradox.

proverbs.literal_en: The tongue has no bone.
proverbs.meaning_en: The tongue turns freely — people say anything.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish half of the shared Greek–Turkish bone image; used of loose or shifting talk.

proverbs.original: جراحات السنان لها التئام، ولا يلتام ما جرح اللسان.
proverbs.transliteration: Jirāḥāt as-sinān lahā iltiʾām, wa-lā yaltām mā jaraḥa al-lisān.
proverbs.literal_en: Wounds of the spearhead can close; what the tongue has wounded does not close.
proverbs.meaning_en: Steel wounds heal; word wounds don't.
proverbs.notes: A classical Arabic verse in universal proverbial use.

proverbs.literal_en: Death and life are in the hand of the tongue.
proverbs.meaning_en: Speech has the power to kill and to give life.
proverbs.notes: Proverbs 18:21 — the oldest datable form of the concept in this cluster.

proverbs.original: زخم زبان از زخم شمشیر بدتر است.
proverbs.transliteration: Zakhm-e zabān az zakhm-e shamshīr badtar ast.
proverbs.literal_en: The tongue's wound is worse than the sword's wound.
proverbs.notes: 'Zakhm-e zabān' — tongue-wound — is a fixed Persian expression for a cutting remark.

proverbs.literal_en: The mouth is the origin of calamity.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form; often quoted as a caution before speaking.

proverbs.literal_en: Calamity comes out of the mouth.
proverbs.notes: Often paired with 病从口入 — 'illness enters by the mouth' — as a couplet.

proverbs.original: La lengua no tiene hueso, pero corta lo más grueso.
proverbs.literal_en: The tongue has no bone, but it cuts the thickest thing.
proverbs.notes: Spanish member of the boneless-tongue family, rhymed hueso/grueso.

proverbs.original: Слово не воробей: вылетит — не поймаешь.
proverbs.transliteration: Slovo ne vorobey: vyletit — ne poymayesh'.
proverbs.literal_en: A word is not a sparrow: once it flies out, you cannot catch it.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; the adjacent Russian insight — the harm of the tongue is irreversible.

concepts.title: Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet
concepts.gloss: Endurance is painful now and rewarded later.
concepts.attestation_source: Proverbial in Persian and Turkish tradition; the French form was popularised by Rousseau's correspondence.

proverbs.original: صبر تلخ است ولیکن بر شیرین دارد.
proverbs.transliteration: Sabr talkh ast valīkan bar-e shīrīn dārad.
proverbs.literal_en: Patience is bitter, but it bears sweet fruit.
proverbs.meaning_en: Endure the bitterness; the harvest is sweet.
proverbs.notes: Classical Persian form of the concept, quoted throughout the Persianate world.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience is bitter; its fruit is sweet.
proverbs.notes: Turkish twin of the Persian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience is the key to relief.
proverbs.notes: One of the central Arabic sayings on ṣabr (steadfast patience), echoing Qur'anic themes.

proverbs.transliteration: Rěn zì tóu shàng yī bǎ dāo.
proverbs.literal_en: The character for 'endure' has a knife above the heart.
proverbs.meaning_en: Patience means holding still under a blade — it hurts by definition.
proverbs.notes: A folk reading of the character 忍: 刃 (blade) over 心 (heart).

proverbs.transliteration: Ishi no ue ni mo san nen.
proverbs.literal_en: Even on a stone — three years.
proverbs.meaning_en: Sit long enough on the cold stone and it warms; persist and the situation yields.
proverbs.notes: The fixed Japanese image of endurance rewarded.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience and labour will grind through everything.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed trud/peretrut; standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience brings roses.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; attested since the 16th century.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience is a fine thing.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: Patience draws blessings.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swahili form; subira is the same Arabic loan (ṣabr) as in the Arabic proverb.

proverbs.original: گر صبر کنی، ز غوره حلوا سازی.
proverbs.transliteration: Gar sabr konī, ze ghūre ḥalvā sāzī.
proverbs.literal_en: If you are patient, you can make halva from sour grapes.
proverbs.meaning_en: Time and patience transmute the sour into the sweet.
proverbs.notes: Classical Persian; the alchemy of patience — unripe grapes become sweet halva.

concepts.title: A drowning man clutches at a straw
concepts.gloss: In desperation, people grasp at even useless or dangerous hopes.
concepts.attestation_source: Thomas More, A Dialogue of Comfort — 'a man in peril of drowning catcheth whatsoever cometh next to hand.'

proverbs.original: A drowning man clutches at a straw.
proverbs.literal_en: A drowning man clutches at a straw.
proverbs.notes: From Thomas More's image (1534), fixed into proverb by the 17th century.

proverbs.literal_en: The drowning man grabs at a little straw.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The drowning man clings to a straw.
proverbs.notes: Standard Arabic form.

proverbs.original: 溺れる者は藁をもつかむ。
proverbs.transliteration: Oboreru mono wa wara o mo tsukamu.
proverbs.literal_en: The drowning person grasps even at straw.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form.

proverbs.literal_en: He who falls into the sea embraces a snake.
proverbs.meaning_en: The desperate will cling even to what can kill them.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish sharpens the straw into a snake — desperation embraces danger itself.

proverbs.literal_en: To grab onto a burning nail.
proverbs.meaning_en: To seize any hope, however painful.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish idiom replaces the straw with a red-hot nail.

proverbs.original: Ο πνιγμένος από τα μαλλιά του πιάνεται.
proverbs.transliteration: O pnigménos apó ta malliá tou piánetai.
proverbs.literal_en: The drowning man grabs hold of his own hair.
proverbs.meaning_en: Desperation clutches even at the useless.
proverbs.notes: The Greek gives the drowning man nothing external at all — only his own hair.

proverbs.literal_en: When the illness is critical, one rushes to any doctor.
proverbs.notes: The Chinese casts the drowning as illness — the desperate patient tries every quack.

concepts.title: Rome wasn't built in a day
concepts.gloss: Great things take long, patient building.
concepts.attestation_source: Medieval French — 'Rome ne fu pas faite toute en un jour' (Li Proverbe au Vilain, c. 1190).

proverbs.original: Rome wasn't built in a day.
proverbs.literal_en: Rome wasn't built in a day.
proverbs.notes: Borrowed from the medieval French; in English by the 16th century.

proverbs.original: Rome ne s'est pas faite en un jour.
proverbs.literal_en: Rome was not made in a day.
proverbs.notes: The oldest attested branch — c. 1190, in the Proverbe au Vilain.

proverbs.original: Roma non fu fatta in un giorno.
proverbs.literal_en: Rome was not made in a day.
proverbs.notes: The Italians say it of their own capital.

proverbs.original: No se ganó Zamora en una hora.
proverbs.literal_en: Zamora was not won in an hour.
proverbs.notes: Spain substitutes its own epic — the long siege of Zamora (1072) — for Rome; rhymed Zamora/hora.

proverbs.original: Rom wurde nicht an einem Tag erbaut.
proverbs.literal_en: Rome was not built in one day.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form of the shared European proverb.

proverbs.transliteration: Bīng dòng sān chǐ, fēi yī rì zhī hán.
proverbs.literal_en: Three feet of ice is not the cold of a single day.
proverbs.meaning_en: Deep states of affairs — good or bad — accumulate slowly.
proverbs.notes: Classical Chinese, with roots in Wang Chong's Lunheng (1st c. CE); used of problems as often as achievements.

proverbs.original: ローマは一日にして成らず。
proverbs.transliteration: Rōma wa ichinichi ni shite narazu.
proverbs.literal_en: Rome was not made in one day.
proverbs.notes: A fully naturalised borrowing — standard in Japanese speech and schoolbooks.

concepts.title: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step
concepts.gloss: Every great undertaking starts with one small act.
concepts.attestation_source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 64 — 千里之行,始于足下.

proverbs.transliteration: Qiān lǐ zhī xíng, shǐ yú zú xià.
proverbs.literal_en: A journey of a thousand li begins beneath one's feet.
proverbs.meaning_en: The greatest undertaking starts with the first step.
proverbs.notes: Tao Te Ching, chapter 64 — the source of the worldwide proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: Even a thousand-li road — from one step.
proverbs.meaning_en: Start small; everything long starts short.
proverbs.notes: The fully nativised Korean form of the Laozi image.

proverbs.transliteration: Senri no michi mo ippo kara.
proverbs.literal_en: Even a road of a thousand ri — from one step.
proverbs.meaning_en: Start small; everything long starts short.
proverbs.notes: The Japanese branch of the same East Asian family.

proverbs.original: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
proverbs.literal_en: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
proverbs.meaning_en: Start small; everything long starts short.
proverbs.notes: A 20th-century English translation of Laozi that has become proverbial in its own right.

concepts.title: Little by little fills the sack
concepts.gloss: Small persistent additions accumulate into great quantities.
concepts.attestation_source: Ovid, Epistulae ex Ponto — 'gutta cavat lapidem' ('the drop hollows the stone'); the accumulation forms are folk-traditional worldwide.

proverbs.original: Many a little makes a mickle.
proverbs.literal_en: Many a little makes a much.
proverbs.notes: Old English/Scots 'mickle' = a great amount; popularised in America by George Washington's use.

proverbs.original: Φασούλι το φασούλι γεμίζει το σακούλι.
proverbs.transliteration: Fasoúli to fasoúli gemízei to sakoúli.
proverbs.literal_en: Bean by bean, the sack fills.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed fasoúli/sakoúli; the standard Greek accumulation proverb.

proverbs.original: Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid.
proverbs.literal_en: Little by little, the bird makes its nest.
proverbs.meaning_en: Steady small work completes the home.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; rhymed petit/nid.

proverbs.literal_en: The constant drop hollows the stone.
proverbs.notes: From Ovid's 'gutta cavat lapidem'; standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Water wears the stone.
proverbs.notes: Russian branch of the Ovidian dripping-stone family.

proverbs.original: De grão em grão, a galinha enche o papo.
proverbs.literal_en: Grain by grain, the hen fills her crop.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form; the hen pecks her way to a full crop.

proverbs.original: Un grano no hace granero, pero ayuda al compañero.
proverbs.literal_en: One grain does not make a granary, but it helps its companion.
proverbs.meaning_en: Each small contribution counts toward the whole.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed granero/compañero; folk-traditional.

proverbs.original: 塵も積もれば山となる。
proverbs.transliteration: Chiri mo tsumoreba yama to naru.
proverbs.literal_en: Even dust, piled up, becomes a mountain.
proverbs.meaning_en: The smallest things accumulate into the greatest.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form; from a Buddhist source tradition.

proverbs.literal_en: Accumulate little, become much.
proverbs.notes: Four-character idiom, standard in Mandarin.

proverbs.literal_en: Little and little fills the measure.
proverbs.notes: The kibaba is a grain measure; one of the best-known Swahili proverbs.

proverbs.original: Sedikit demi sedikit, lama-lama menjadi bukit.
proverbs.literal_en: Little by little, in time it becomes a hill.
proverbs.meaning_en: Small persistent additions build something visible.
proverbs.notes: Standard Indonesian/Malay form; rhymed sedikit/bukit.

proverbs.literal_en: Drop by drop, a lake forms.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Many littles go to a lot.
proverbs.notes: Standard Hungarian form.

concepts.title: Practice makes the master
concepts.gloss: Skill is built by repetition, not talent.
concepts.attestation_source: German 'Übung macht den Meister' attested from the 16th century; Latin 'usus magister est optimus' (Cicero) is the classical ancestor.

proverbs.literal_en: Practice makes perfect.
proverbs.notes: In English since the 16th century ('use makes mastery' in older forms).

proverbs.literal_en: Practice makes the master.
proverbs.notes: The German form crowns a master, not perfection — a guild culture speaking.

proverbs.original: C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron.
proverbs.literal_en: It is by forging that one becomes a blacksmith.
proverbs.meaning_en: You become the craftsman by doing the craft.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; the trade itself is the school.

proverbs.literal_en: Practice makes the master.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Familiarity can give birth to skill.
proverbs.notes: Standard chengyu; linked to the Song-era tale of the old oil-seller pouring through a coin's hole.

proverbs.literal_en: Rather than be taught — get used to it.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form; experience over lessons.

proverbs.literal_en: Repetition is the mother of learning.
proverbs.meaning_en: You learn by going over it again.
proverbs.notes: From the Latin school maxim 'repetitio est mater studiorum'.

proverbs.literal_en: Practice begets art.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: By erring, one learns.
proverbs.meaning_en: Mistakes are the tuition of skill.
proverbs.notes: The Italian shifts the emphasis from repetition to error — you learn by getting it wrong.

proverbs.literal_en: Exercise makes the master.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form, cognate with the German.

proverbs.literal_en: Practice makes the master.
proverbs.notes: Standard Hungarian form.

concepts.title: All that glitters is not gold
concepts.gloss: Attractive surfaces often conceal worthless substance.
concepts.attestation_source: Medieval Latin 'non omne quod nitet aurum est'; Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice — 'all that glisters is not gold.'

proverbs.original: All that glitters is not gold.
proverbs.literal_en: All that glitters is not gold.
proverbs.notes: Shakespeare's 'glisters' (Merchant of Venice, 1596) modernised to 'glitters'; the Latin is centuries older.

proverbs.original: Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or.
proverbs.literal_en: All that shines is not gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: Es ist nicht alles Gold, was glänzt.
proverbs.literal_en: Not everything that gleams is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.original: No es oro todo lo que reluce.
proverbs.literal_en: Not all that shines is gold.
proverbs.notes: Used by Cervantes in Don Quixote.

proverbs.original: Non è tutto oro quel che luccica.
proverbs.literal_en: Not all that sparkles is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Не всё то золото, что блестит.
proverbs.transliteration: Ne vsyo to zoloto, chto blestit.
proverbs.literal_en: Not all is gold that glitters.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Nem tudo que reluz é ouro.
proverbs.literal_en: Not everything that shines is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.original: Nie wszystko złoto, co się świeci.
proverbs.literal_en: Not everything is gold that shines.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: Het is niet al goud wat er blinkt.
proverbs.literal_en: It is not all gold that gleams.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.original: Nu tot ce strălucește e aur.
proverbs.literal_en: Not all that glitters is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Romanian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Not everything that shines is gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Whatever shines is not gold.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.original: हर चमकती चीज़ सोना नहीं होती।
proverbs.transliteration: Har chamaktī chīz sonā nahīṉ hotī.
proverbs.literal_en: Every shining thing is not gold.
proverbs.notes: The standard Hindi rendering, fully naturalised in everyday speech.

concepts.title: When the cat's away, the mice will play
concepts.gloss: When authority is absent, the supervised run free.
concepts.attestation_source: Medieval French 'ou chat na rat regne'; English form proverbial by the 16th century.

proverbs.original: When the cat's away, the mice will play.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat's away, the mice will play.
proverbs.notes: Proverbial in English since at least the 1600s.

proverbs.original: Quand le chat n'est pas là, les souris dansent.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is not there, the mice dance.
proverbs.notes: The French mice dance rather than play.

proverbs.original: Ist die Katze aus dem Haus, tanzen die Mäuse auf dem Tisch.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is out of the house, the mice dance on the table.
proverbs.notes: The German mice go one further — onto the table.

proverbs.original: Cuando el gato no está, los ratones bailan.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is not there, the mice dance.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.original: Quando il gatto non c'è, i topi ballano.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat isn't there, the mice dance.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.original: Als de kat van huis is, dansen de muizen op tafel.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is away from home, the mice dance on the table.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.original: Кот из дома — мыши в пляс.
proverbs.transliteration: Kot iz doma — myshi v plyas.
proverbs.literal_en: Cat out of the house — mice into dance.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: 山中无老虎,猴子称大王。
proverbs.transliteration: Shān zhōng wú lǎohǔ, hóuzi chēng dàwáng.
proverbs.literal_en: With no tiger in the mountains, the monkey declares himself king.
proverbs.meaning_en: In the absence of the strong, the mediocre rule.
proverbs.notes: A different angle on absent authority: not mischief but usurpation.

proverbs.transliteration: Oni no inu ma ni sentaku.
proverbs.literal_en: Laundry while the demon is away.
proverbs.meaning_en: Seize the tyrant's absence to breathe — 'washing' here is washing one's spirit.
proverbs.notes: The 'oni' (demon) is the household tyrant; the laundry is proverbially a laundering of the heart (命の洗濯).

proverbs.original: Όταν λείπει η γάτα, χορεύουν τα ποντίκια.
proverbs.transliteration: Ótan leípei i gáta, chorévoun ta pontíkia.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is missing, the mice dance.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Greek form.

proverbs.original: Gdy kota nie ma, myszy harcują.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is gone, the mice frolic.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: Kun kissa on poissa, hiiret hyppivät pöydällä.
proverbs.literal_en: When the cat is away, the mice jump on the table.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

concepts.title: Two birds with one stone
concepts.gloss: One action achieving two goals at once.
concepts.attestation_source: Book of Sui / History of the Northern Dynasties — the archer Zhangsun Sheng downs two eagles with one arrow (一箭双雕).

proverbs.original: To kill two birds with one stone.
proverbs.literal_en: To kill two birds with one stone.
proverbs.notes: In English since the 17th century.

proverbs.literal_en: One arrow, a pair of eagles.
proverbs.notes: From the historical feat of the archer Zhangsun Sheng (6th c.), recorded in the dynastic histories.

proverbs.literal_en: One stone, two birds.
proverbs.notes: A four-character idiom formed in Japanese from the English proverb — a rare reverse borrowing.

proverbs.original: Zwei Fliegen mit einer Klappe schlagen.
proverbs.literal_en: To hit two flies with one swat.
proverbs.notes: The German scales the game down to flies and a fly-swat.

proverbs.literal_en: To make two strikes with one stone.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form — the stone without the birds.

proverbs.original: Matar dos pájaros de un tiro.
proverbs.literal_en: To kill two birds with one shot.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish upgrades the stone to a gunshot.

proverbs.original: Prendere due piccioni con una fava.
proverbs.literal_en: To catch two pigeons with one broad bean.
proverbs.notes: The Italian baits two pigeons with a single bean — capture, not killing.

proverbs.literal_en: To kill two hares with one shot.
proverbs.notes: Russian hunts hares instead of birds; often just 'убить двух зайцев'.

proverbs.original: Matar dois coelhos com uma cajadada só.
proverbs.literal_en: To kill two rabbits with a single blow of the staff.
proverbs.notes: The Portuguese wields a shepherd's staff against two rabbits.

proverbs.literal_en: To hit two birds with one stone.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: With one shot, two turtledoves.
proverbs.notes: 'Σμπάρος' is a Venetian loan for a gunshot — a trace of the Ionian islands in the proverb.

proverbs.original: Upiec dwie pieczenie na jednym ogniu.
proverbs.literal_en: To roast two roasts on one fire.
proverbs.notes: The Polish version cooks instead of hunting.

proverbs.literal_en: Two flies with one strike.
proverbs.notes: Finnish follows the German fly version.

proverbs.literal_en: While diving, drink water.
proverbs.meaning_en: Accomplish a second goal inside the first action.
proverbs.notes: The Indonesian image is peaceable — no creature is harmed; the diver simply drinks.

concepts.title: Birds of a feather flock together
concepts.gloss: Like seeks like; people gather with their own kind.
concepts.attestation_source: Ancient Greek 'ὅμοιος ὁμοίῳ ἀεὶ πελάζει' (like ever draws near to like) — Homer's Odyssey XVII and Plato's Symposium carry versions.

proverbs.original: Birds of a feather flock together.
proverbs.literal_en: Birds of a feather flock together.
proverbs.meaning_en: The similar seek each other out.
proverbs.notes: In English since the mid-16th century.

proverbs.literal_en: Like ever draws near to like.
proverbs.notes: Ancient Greek, echoed in Homer (Odyssey XVII.218) and quoted by Plato; still cited in modern Greek.

proverbs.literal_en: A fisherman spots a fisherman from afar.
proverbs.meaning_en: Kindred spirits recognise each other instantly.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: A kind calls its friends.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form.

proverbs.transliteration: Wù yǐ lèi jù, rén yǐ qún fēn.
proverbs.literal_en: Things gather by kind; people divide by group.
proverbs.meaning_en: Everything and everyone sorts itself by likeness.
proverbs.notes: From the Yijing commentary tradition via the Warring States texts.

proverbs.original: Gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern.
proverbs.literal_en: Like and like keep company gladly.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Those who resemble each other assemble.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed ressemble/assemble; standard French form.

proverbs.original: Dios los cría y ellos se juntan.
proverbs.literal_en: God raises them, and they find each other.
proverbs.meaning_en: The similar will meet — usually said disapprovingly.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form; almost always ironic.

proverbs.literal_en: Who resemble each other, take each other.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed somiglia/piglia; used of couples especially.

proverbs.literal_en: The pot rolled and found its lid.
proverbs.meaning_en: Everyone finds their matching other — usually said wryly.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form; typically of well-matched (often badly-behaved) pairs.

proverbs.literal_en: Birds land on their own kinds.
proverbs.notes: The Arabic bird form, independent of the English one.

proverbs.literal_en: A kind has found its kind.
proverbs.meaning_en: Like has met like — said when two of a type join up.
proverbs.notes: Talmudic idiom in continuous proverbial use.

proverbs.literal_en: Kind follows kind.
proverbs.notes: Sino-Korean four-character idiom (類類相從) in everyday use.

proverbs.literal_en: One's own is drawn to one's own.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

concepts.title: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder
concepts.gloss: Attractiveness and taste are judgments of the viewer, not properties of the thing.
concepts.attestation_source: Margaret Wolfe Hungerford, Molly Bawn (1878); the idea is classical (Theocritus) and worldwide.

proverbs.original: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
proverbs.literal_en: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
proverbs.meaning_en: Beauty is conferred by the viewer.
proverbs.notes: Wording fixed by Margaret Wolfe Hungerford (1878); the sentiment is ancient.

proverbs.literal_en: The monkey, in its mother's eye, is a gazelle.
proverbs.meaning_en: Love re-sees the plain as beautiful.
proverbs.notes: One of the most-quoted Egyptian proverbs; affectionately mocking.

proverbs.literal_en: To the raven, its chick looks like a falcon.
proverbs.meaning_en: A parent's eye upgrades its own.
proverbs.notes: The Turkish twin of the Arabic monkey/gazelle image, with birds.

proverbs.literal_en: Even the insects that eat knotweed do so by preference.
proverbs.meaning_en: There is no accounting for taste — some creatures choose the bitter plant.
proverbs.notes: Tade (water pepper) is proverbially acrid; the standard Japanese form for subjective taste.

proverbs.original: Des goûts et des couleurs, on ne discute pas.
proverbs.literal_en: About tastes and colours, one does not argue.
proverbs.notes: The French descendant of the scholastic Latin 'de gustibus non est disputandum'.

proverbs.original: Sobre gustos no hay nada escrito.
proverbs.literal_en: About tastes, nothing is written.
proverbs.meaning_en: There is no law of taste.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form — no rulebook exists for preference.

proverbs.literal_en: In a lover's eyes appears Xi Shi.
proverbs.meaning_en: The beloved becomes the legendary beauty.
proverbs.notes: Xi Shi was one of the Four Beauties of ancient China; the lover's eye produces her.

proverbs.original: لیلی را از چشم مجنون باید دید.
proverbs.transliteration: Leylī rā az cheshm-e Majnūn bāyad dīd.
proverbs.literal_en: Layla must be seen through Majnun's eyes.
proverbs.meaning_en: Only the lover's gaze reveals the beloved's beauty.
proverbs.notes: From the Layla and Majnun romance tradition; fully proverbial in Persian.

concepts.title: A crow does not peck out another crow's eye
concepts.gloss: Members of the same group spare each other — insiders protect insiders.
concepts.attestation_source: Macrobius, Saturnalia — 'cornix cornici oculos non effodit.'

proverbs.literal_en: There is honour among thieves.
proverbs.meaning_en: Even the lawless keep faith with their own.
proverbs.notes: English casts the in-group solidarity concept with thieves rather than crows.

proverbs.literal_en: A raven will not peck out a raven's eye.
proverbs.meaning_en: Insiders don't harm insiders — said of cliques and corrupt elites.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form of the Latin crow proverb.

proverbs.original: Eine Krähe hackt der anderen kein Auge aus.
proverbs.literal_en: One crow does not hack out another's eye.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; almost always said of professions closing ranks.

proverbs.original: Les loups ne se mangent pas entre eux.
proverbs.literal_en: Wolves do not eat each other.
proverbs.notes: The French replaces crows with wolves.

proverbs.literal_en: Dog does not eat dog.
proverbs.notes: From the Latin 'canis caninam non est'; the source of the English 'dog eat dog' by inversion.

proverbs.literal_en: A raven will not gouge out a raven's eye.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: A crow does not peck out a crow's eyes.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form.

proverbs.literal_en: A dog does not bite a dog.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form, with dogs.

concepts.title: God helps those who help themselves
concepts.gloss: Divine or lucky aid comes only to those already acting.
concepts.attestation_source: Aesop, 'Hercules and the Waggoner'; English wording in Algernon Sidney, popularised by Benjamin Franklin (1736).

proverbs.original: God helps those who help themselves.
proverbs.literal_en: God helps those who help themselves.
proverbs.notes: Aesop's carter is told by Hercules to put his own shoulder to the wheel; Franklin fixed the English wording.

proverbs.literal_en: With Athena — move your hand too.
proverbs.meaning_en: Invoke the goddess, but also act.
proverbs.notes: The ancient Greek fable moral (the shipwrecked man told to swim as he prays); still quoted in modern Greece.

proverbs.literal_en: Help yourself, and heaven will help you.
proverbs.notes: Fixed by La Fontaine, 'Le Chartier embourbé' (1668) — the same Aesopic carter.

proverbs.literal_en: Tie her (the camel) — and trust in God.
proverbs.meaning_en: Faith does not replace precaution; do both.
proverbs.notes: From the hadith of the man who asked whether to tether his camel or trust God (Tirmidhi).

proverbs.original: На Бога надейся, а сам не плошай.
proverbs.transliteration: Na Boga nadeysya, a sam ne ploshay.
proverbs.literal_en: Hope in God — but don't slack yourself.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Hilf dir selbst, so hilft dir Gott.
proverbs.literal_en: Help yourself, so God helps you.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; proverbial since the Reformation era.

proverbs.original: A Dios rogando y con el mazo dando.
proverbs.literal_en: Praying to God — and striking with the mallet.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed rogando/dando; the mallet is a craftsman's — prayer and work in the same breath.

concepts.title: Forbidden fruit is sweetest
concepts.gloss: Prohibition itself makes a thing desirable.
concepts.attestation_source: English proverbial form recorded in the 17th century; the image descends from Genesis 3.

proverbs.literal_en: Forbidden fruit is sweetest.
proverbs.notes: From the Eden narrative of Genesis 3, proverbial in English by the 1660s.

proverbs.literal_en: The forbidden fruit is sweet.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Forbidden fruits taste best.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Prohibition brings craving.
proverbs.meaning_en: Forbidding a thing creates appetite for it.
proverbs.notes: Persian states the psychology plainly, without the fruit.

concepts.title: Hunger is the best sauce
concepts.gloss: Need makes everything satisfying; appetite is the true seasoning.
concepts.attestation_source: Cicero, De Finibus II — 'cibi condimentum esse famem' ('hunger is the seasoning of food'), reporting Socrates.

proverbs.literal_en: Hunger is the best sauce.
proverbs.notes: From the Socratic saying reported by Cicero.

proverbs.literal_en: Hunger is the best cook.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; attested since the Middle Ages.

proverbs.original: A buen hambre no hay pan duro.
proverbs.literal_en: To a good hunger there is no hard bread.
proverbs.meaning_en: The hungry find no fault with food.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.original: À la faim, tout est pain.
proverbs.literal_en: To hunger, everything is bread.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed faim/pain; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: Hunger is not an aunt.
proverbs.meaning_en: Hunger shows no kindness — it forces you to act.
proverbs.notes: The full older form adds '…пирожка не подсунет' — 'it won't slip you a little pie' like an aunt would.

proverbs.literal_en: Hunger is the best spice.
proverbs.notes: Standard Finnish form.

proverbs.original: Is maith an t-anlann an t-ocras.
proverbs.literal_en: Hunger is a good sauce.
proverbs.notes: One of the most familiar Irish-language proverbs, taught to every school-child.

concepts.title: All beginnings are difficult
concepts.gloss: The start is the hardest part — and half the work.
concepts.first_attested: ~3rd century CE (Hebrew); ancient Greek 'half of the whole'
concepts.attestation_source: Mekhilta de-Rabbi Ishmael — 'kol hatchalot kashot'; Greek 'ἀρχὴ ἥμισυ παντός' attributed to Pythagoras (via Iamblichus).

proverbs.literal_en: Every beginning is hard.
proverbs.notes: The standard German form, proverbial since Luther's era.

proverbs.literal_en: All beginnings are difficult.
proverbs.notes: From the Mekhilta (midrash on Exodus); in continuous Hebrew use for ~1800 years.

proverbs.original: Η αρχή είναι το ήμισυ του παντός.
proverbs.transliteration: I archí eínai to ímisy tou pantós.
proverbs.literal_en: The beginning is half of the whole.
proverbs.meaning_en: To have begun is to be half done.
proverbs.notes: Attributed to Pythagoras; the Latin 'dimidium facti qui coepit habet' (Horace) is its echo.

proverbs.literal_en: The beginning is half.
proverbs.notes: The Korean twin of the Pythagorean maxim; among the most-used Korean proverbs.

proverbs.literal_en: In ten thousand affairs, the opening is hard.
proverbs.meaning_en: Everything is hardest at the start.
proverbs.notes: Standard Mandarin form.

proverbs.original: Il n'y a que le premier pas qui coûte.
proverbs.literal_en: Only the first step costs.
proverbs.meaning_en: After the start, the rest follows.
proverbs.notes: Made famous by Mme du Deffand's quip (1763) about the legend of St Denis walking with his head in his hands.

proverbs.literal_en: The fierce trouble is the beginning.
proverbs.meaning_en: The start is the only real obstacle.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; compact and idiomatic.

proverbs.original: 案ずるより産むが易し。
proverbs.literal_en: Giving birth is easier than worrying about it.
proverbs.meaning_en: The dread of beginning is worse than the deed.
proverbs.notes: From midwives' reassurance; the standard Japanese form for fears that outweigh facts.

concepts.title: Don't cry over spilled milk
concepts.gloss: What is done cannot be undone — regret changes nothing.
concepts.attestation_source: James Howell's proverb collection (1659) — 'no weeping for shed milk'; the Chinese spilled-water story is ~11 centuries older.

proverbs.original: It's no use crying over spilled milk.
proverbs.literal_en: It's no use crying over spilled milk.
proverbs.meaning_en: Regret over the irreversible is wasted.
proverbs.notes: Howell (1659): 'no weeping for shed milk.'

proverbs.literal_en: Spilled water is hard to gather back.
proverbs.notes: From the story of Jiang Taigong (Lü Shang), whose wife begged to return after his rise — he poured out water and asked her to regather it.

proverbs.literal_en: Spilled water does not return to the tray.
proverbs.notes: The Japanese branch of the same Chinese story.

proverbs.literal_en: With tears, you won't help the sorrow.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: To what is done — chest.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed hecho/pecho; the Spanish answer is posture, not grief.

proverbs.literal_en: Water gone by grinds no more.
proverbs.meaning_en: The past has no more power — let it go.
proverbs.notes: A miller's image: water past the wheel can turn nothing.

proverbs.literal_en: The last regret is of no use.
proverbs.meaning_en: Regret after the fact repairs nothing.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: What was — was.
proverbs.meaning_en: The past is closed; move on.
proverbs.notes: Everyday Hebrew formula of acceptance, proverbial in force.

concepts.title: Cheap turns out expensive
concepts.gloss: Skimping costs more in the end.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-commercial wisdom across many cultures; English 'penny wise and pound foolish' recorded by E. Topsell, 1607.

proverbs.literal_en: Penny wise, pound foolish.
proverbs.meaning_en: Careful with small sums, wasteful with large ones.
proverbs.notes: Recorded from 1607; the classic English form of false economy.

proverbs.literal_en: The miser pays twice.
proverbs.meaning_en: Cheap purchases must be bought again.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The cheap turns out expensive.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: The cheap comes out expensive.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.literal_en: Who buys cheap, buys expensive.
proverbs.meaning_en: The cheap purchase is the costly one.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Cheap-buy is dear-buy.
proverbs.meaning_en: The cheap purchase is the costly one.
proverbs.notes: A compact Dutch compound-word proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: Cheap has no good goods.
proverbs.notes: Often completed: 好货不便宜 — 'good goods are not cheap.'

proverbs.literal_en: The stew of cheap meat turns out flavourless.
proverbs.meaning_en: Skimp on the ingredient, ruin the dish.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form; the proof is in the stew.

concepts.title: No rose without a thorn
concepts.gloss: Every pleasure carries its pain; nothing good is unmixed.
concepts.attestation_source: Proverbial across Europe and the Persian world since the Middle Ages; a fixture of Persian rose-and-nightingale poetry.

proverbs.literal_en: No rose without a thorn.
proverbs.meaning_en: Every good comes with its cost.
proverbs.notes: In English collections from the 16th century.

proverbs.literal_en: No rose without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.original: Il n'y a pas de roses sans épines.
proverbs.literal_en: There are no roses without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no flower without a thorn.
proverbs.notes: In Persian, 'gol' (flower) means above all the rose — the heart of Persian poetry.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no thornless rose.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form; often applied to love.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no rose without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no rose without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no rose without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: There is no rose without thorns.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

concepts.title: As you sow, so shall you reap
concepts.gloss: Consequences follow conduct; you harvest what you plant.
concepts.attestation_source: Epistle to the Galatians 6:7 — 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap'; Hosea 8:7 for the wind/whirlwind form.

proverbs.literal_en: You reap what you sow.
proverbs.meaning_en: Your outcomes are your own planting.
proverbs.notes: From Galatians 6:7 in the English Bible tradition.

proverbs.literal_en: Whatever you sow, you will reap.
proverbs.notes: The Greek of Galatians 6:7 ('ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει') in its modern proverbial form.

proverbs.literal_en: What you sow is what you will reap.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Wie die Saat, so die Ernte.
proverbs.literal_en: As the seed, so the harvest.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.transliteration: Zhòng guā dé guā, zhòng dòu dé dòu.
proverbs.literal_en: Plant melons, get melons; plant beans, get beans.
proverbs.meaning_en: Each deed yields exactly its own kind.
proverbs.notes: The paired-crop form is the standard Chinese casting, with Buddhist karmic overtones.

proverbs.literal_en: One's own karma, one's own gain.
proverbs.meaning_en: You suffer (or enjoy) the results of your own deeds — usually said of deserved misfortune.
proverbs.notes: A Buddhist four-character term fully proverbialised in Japanese.

proverbs.literal_en: As the doing, so the filling.
proverbs.meaning_en: As you act, so you are repaid.
proverbs.notes: The rhymed Hindi form of the karmic harvest.

proverbs.literal_en: Whatever you sow, that you mow.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Who sows, reaps.
proverbs.meaning_en: Effort and conduct come back to you.
proverbs.notes: Compressed classical Arabic form; often expanded 'man zaraʿa khayran ḥaṣada khayran' — who sows good reaps good.

proverbs.original: Qui sème le vent récolte la tempête.
proverbs.literal_en: Who sows the wind harvests the storm.
proverbs.meaning_en: Sow harm and reap it multiplied.
proverbs.notes: From Hosea 8:7; the negative, escalating branch of the sowing family.

proverbs.literal_en: Who sows winds gathers storms.
proverbs.meaning_en: Sow harm and reap it multiplied.
proverbs.notes: The Spanish branch of the Hosea wind/whirlwind image.

proverbs.original: Jak sobie pościelesz, tak się wyśpisz.
proverbs.literal_en: As you make your bed, so you will sleep.
proverbs.notes: The bed-making variant — same logic, domestic image; shared with English 'you've made your bed…'.

concepts.title: All roads lead to Rome
concepts.gloss: Many different paths arrive at the same destination.
concepts.attestation_source: Alain de Lille, Liber Parabolarum — 'mille viae ducunt homines per saecula Romam' ('a thousand roads lead men forever to Rome').

proverbs.literal_en: All roads lead to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: From the medieval Latin of Alain de Lille; grounded in the literal Roman road network.

proverbs.original: Tous les chemins mènent à Rome.
proverbs.literal_en: All roads lead to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form; La Fontaine used it in his fables.

proverbs.literal_en: All ways lead to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.original: Tutte le strade portano a Roma.
proverbs.literal_en: All the roads carry to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form — said of the literal capital.

proverbs.original: Todos los caminos llevan a Roma.
proverbs.literal_en: All the roads lead to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: All roads lead to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Every great road goes through to Rome.
proverbs.meaning_en: Different methods reach the same end.
proverbs.notes: A fully naturalised borrowing, extremely common in modern Chinese; the native equivalent is 殊途同归 — 'different routes, same return.'

concepts.title: Fall seven times, rise eight
concepts.gloss: Persistence through repeated failure is the path to success.
concepts.attestation_source: Japanese 七転び八起き, associated with the self-righting Daruma doll tradition.

proverbs.literal_en: Seven falls, eight risings.
proverbs.meaning_en: However often you fall, get up once more than you fell.
proverbs.notes: Embodied in the Daruma doll, weighted to right itself when knocked over.

proverbs.original: If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
proverbs.literal_en: If at first you don't succeed, try, try again.
proverbs.meaning_en: Failure is an instruction to repeat.
proverbs.notes: Popularised by W. E. Hickson's 19th-century schoolbook verse.

proverbs.literal_en: Failure is the mother of success.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Chinese form.

proverbs.original: Có công mài sắt, có ngày nên kim.
proverbs.literal_en: With effort grinding iron, one day it becomes a needle.
proverbs.meaning_en: Relentless patient work achieves the seemingly impossible.
proverbs.notes: The Vietnamese branch of the East Asian iron-pestle-to-needle tradition (Chinese 铁杵磨成针, told of the poet Li Bai).

proverbs.literal_en: An attempt is not torture.
proverbs.notes: The rhyme popytka/pytka carries it; standard encouragement to make the attempt.

concepts.title: Old ginger is spicier — the worth of experience
concepts.gloss: Age and experience outperform youthful vigour.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-traditional in each culture; no single classical source.

proverbs.literal_en: Ginger — it's still the old that's spicy.
proverbs.meaning_en: The veteran has the sharper bite.
proverbs.notes: Said admiringly when an old hand outdoes the young.

proverbs.original: Más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo.
proverbs.literal_en: The devil knows more from being old than from being the devil.
proverbs.meaning_en: Experience, not talent, is the deepest knowledge.
proverbs.notes: One of the most-quoted Spanish proverbs on age.

proverbs.transliteration: Kame no kō yori toshi no kō.
proverbs.literal_en: Better than the tortoise's shell is the merit of years.
proverbs.meaning_en: Long experience outvalues even legendary longevity.
proverbs.notes: A pun on kō (甲 shell / 功 merit); the tortoise is the emblem of ten thousand years.

proverbs.literal_en: The old horse will not spoil the furrow.
proverbs.meaning_en: The experienced can be trusted with the delicate work.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; often completed '…но и глубоко не вспашет' — 'but neither will it plough deep.'

proverbs.original: C'est dans les vieux pots qu'on fait les meilleures soupes.
proverbs.literal_en: It is in the old pots that the best soups are made.
proverbs.meaning_en: The seasoned vessel — the seasoned person — produces the best results.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; often said with a wink.

proverbs.literal_en: An old hen makes good broth.
proverbs.notes: Folk-traditional; affectionately applied to people as well as poultry.

concepts.title: Don't teach the expert their own trade
concepts.gloss: Instructing a master in their own art is absurd.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-traditional in each culture; the Chinese form references the master carpenter Lu Ban (5th c. BCE).

proverbs.original: Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't instruct someone in what they've done all their life.
proverbs.notes: In English since the early 18th century (Swift's era).

proverbs.literal_en: Wielding the axe at Lu Ban's gate.
proverbs.meaning_en: Showing off a skill before its greatest master.
proverbs.notes: Lu Ban is the legendary master carpenter; also used self-deprecatingly before showing one's work.

proverbs.literal_en: Preaching the dharma to the Buddha.
proverbs.meaning_en: Lecturing the ultimate authority on their own subject.
proverbs.notes: Standard Japanese form; used with wry apology.

proverbs.original: On n'apprend pas à un vieux singe à faire la grimace.
proverbs.literal_en: One does not teach an old monkey to make faces.
proverbs.meaning_en: The old hand knows every trick you could show them.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: You can't sell cress to the cress-seller.
proverbs.meaning_en: Don't peddle expertise to the expert.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form; a market proverb.

proverbs.original: Das Ei will klüger sein als die Henne.
proverbs.literal_en: The egg wants to be smarter than the hen.
proverbs.meaning_en: The junior presumes to instruct the senior.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form; said of presumptuous juniors.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't teach the taught.
proverbs.notes: Compressed Russian form; often a curt retort.

concepts.title: Man proposes, God disposes
concepts.gloss: Human plans are subject to forces beyond human control.
concepts.attestation_source: Thomas à Kempis, De Imitatione Christi I.19 — 'homo proponit, sed Deus disponit.'

proverbs.literal_en: Man proposes, God disposes.
proverbs.notes: From Thomas à Kempis's Latin (c. 1420), itself echoing Proverbs 16:9.

proverbs.original: דער מענטש טראַכט און גאָט לאַכט.
proverbs.transliteration: Der mentsh trakht un Got lakht.
proverbs.literal_en: Man thinks and God laughs.
proverbs.notes: The most famous of all Yiddish proverbs; the rhyme trakht/lakht carries its shrug.

proverbs.literal_en: Man thinks, God steers.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed denkt/lenkt; the German branch of the Kempis Latin.

proverbs.literal_en: Man proposes and God disposes.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: El hombre propone y Dios dispone.
proverbs.literal_en: Man proposes and God disposes.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Man supposes, and God disposes.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.transliteration: Móu shì zài rén, chéng shì zài tiān.
proverbs.literal_en: Planning affairs lies with man; completing them lies with Heaven.
proverbs.meaning_en: Effort is ours; outcomes are Heaven's.
proverbs.notes: Fixed in the Romance of the Three Kingdoms — Zhuge Liang's words when rain quenches his fire attack.

proverbs.original: Człowiek strzela, Pan Bóg kule nosi.
proverbs.literal_en: Man shoots — the Lord God carries the bullets.
proverbs.meaning_en: You pull the trigger, but where it lands is not yours to decide.
proverbs.notes: The strikingly ballistic Polish form of the concept.

proverbs.original: العبد في التفكير والرب في التدبير.
proverbs.transliteration: Al-ʿabd fī at-tafkīr wa-r-rabb fī at-tadbīr.
proverbs.literal_en: The servant is in the thinking; the Lord is in the arranging.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed tafkīr/tadbīr; standard Arabic form.

concepts.title: East or west, home is best
concepts.gloss: One's own home, however humble, is the best place.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-traditional across cultures; English 'home is home, though it be never so homely' recorded 1546 (Heywood).

proverbs.original: East or west, home is best.
proverbs.literal_en: East or west, home is best.
proverbs.notes: The rhymed 19th-century form; Heywood's 1546 collection has the older 'home is home…'.

proverbs.literal_en: East west, home best.
proverbs.notes: The compact Dutch original of the rhymed east/west form.

proverbs.literal_en: One's own hearth is worth gold.
proverbs.meaning_en: Having your own home is true wealth.
proverbs.notes: Rhymed Herd/wert; standard German form.

proverbs.original: В гостях хорошо, а дома лучше.
proverbs.transliteration: V gostyakh khorosho, a doma luchshe.
proverbs.literal_en: Visiting is good, but home is better.
proverbs.meaning_en: Hospitality is fine — home is finer.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: If you live there, it becomes the capital.
proverbs.meaning_en: Any place becomes home — becomes the best place — once you live in it.
proverbs.notes: The Japanese inverts the cluster: home is not a fixed best place; dwelling makes a place best.

proverbs.original: Wszędzie dobrze, ale w domu najlepiej.
proverbs.literal_en: Everywhere is good, but at home is best.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Everywhere good, at home best.
proverbs.notes: Standard Czech form.

proverbs.literal_en: Away is good, but home is best.
proverbs.notes: Standard Swedish form.

proverbs.literal_en: One's own home, dear as gold.
proverbs.notes: Alliterative Finnish form (koti/kullan/kallis).

proverbs.original: Níl aon tinteán mar do thinteán féin.
proverbs.literal_en: There is no hearth like your own hearth.
proverbs.notes: One of the best-known Irish-language proverbs — famously echoed as 'there's no place like home.'

proverbs.original: Σπίτι μου, σπιτάκι μου, φτωχοκαλυβάκι μου.
proverbs.transliteration: Spíti mou, spitáki mou, ftochokalyváki mou.
proverbs.literal_en: My house, my little house, my poor little hut.
proverbs.meaning_en: However humble, my own home is dearest.
proverbs.notes: A folk rhyme functioning as a proverb; the diminutives do the loving.

proverbs.original: Casa mia, casa mia, per piccina che tu sia, tu mi sembri una badia.
proverbs.literal_en: My house, my house, however tiny you are, you seem an abbey to me.
proverbs.meaning_en: One's own small home feels palatial.
proverbs.notes: A rhymed folk verse in fully proverbial use.

concepts.title: Love is blind
concepts.gloss: Love does not see faults — it transfigures its object.
concepts.attestation_source: Chaucer, The Merchant's Tale — 'for love is blynd al day and may nat see'; the idea is classical (Theocritus, Plato).

proverbs.literal_en: Love is blind.
proverbs.notes: Chaucer first in English; Shakespeare repeated it in three plays.

proverbs.literal_en: Love is blind.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: Love makes blind.
proverbs.meaning_en: Love actively blinds — the German gives it agency.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.literal_en: Love is blind.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Love is blind.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Eros is blind.
proverbs.notes: Modern Greek keeps the classical distinction — it is eros, not agape, that is blind.

proverbs.literal_en: Love is cruel — you could fall for a goat.
proverbs.meaning_en: Love ignores all merit; anyone can be its object.
proverbs.notes: The rhyme zla/kozla makes it the most quoted — and funniest — Russian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Your love of a thing blinds and deafens.
proverbs.meaning_en: Attachment disables both sight and hearing.
proverbs.notes: Transmitted as a hadith (Abu Dawud); proverbial across the Arab world.

proverbs.literal_en: In the lover's eye appears Xi Shi.
proverbs.notes: Xi Shi, one of the Four Beauties; the positive casting of love's blindness.

proverbs.literal_en: Love is blind.
proverbs.notes: Standard modern Persian form; the classical tradition prefers Layla-and-Majnun imagery.

concepts.title: Better safe than sorry
concepts.gloss: Precaution costs less than the disaster it prevents.
concepts.attestation_source: English wording from Samuel Lover's Rory O'More (1837, 'better sure than sorry'); the prevention/cure form is medieval Latin.

proverbs.literal_en: Better safe than sorry.
proverbs.notes: Alongside 'an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure' (Franklin's phrasing of the medieval maxim).

proverbs.literal_en: Preventing is worth more than curing.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form of the medieval Latin 'melius est praevenire quam praeveniri'.

proverbs.literal_en: Better to prevent than to heal.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.literal_en: To prevent is better than to cure.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: Preventing is better than healing.
proverbs.notes: Standard Dutch form.

proverbs.literal_en: A cane before you fall.
proverbs.meaning_en: Arrange the support before the stumble.
proverbs.notes: The cane taken in advance — the standard Japanese image of precaution.

proverbs.literal_en: Even a stone bridge — tap it before crossing.
proverbs.notes: Korean twin of the Japanese stone-bridge proverb.

proverbs.literal_en: God protects the protected.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form — grace flows to those already being careful.

proverbs.original: Vorsicht ist die Mutter der Porzellankiste.
proverbs.literal_en: Caution is the mother of the china crate.
proverbs.meaning_en: Care is what keeps fragile things whole.
proverbs.notes: A movers' proverb — the crate of porcelain survives by caution alone.

proverbs.literal_en: With preparation, no calamity.
proverbs.notes: From the Book of Documents (Shangshu) via the Zuo Zhuan.

proverbs.literal_en: Better to blow on the cold.
proverbs.meaning_en: Over-caution beats regret — blow even on what isn't hot.
proverbs.notes: The Polish inverts the burnt-child image: blow on cold things, just in case.

concepts.title: Asking is a moment's shame; not asking, a lifetime's
concepts.gloss: Questions cost a little pride and gain the road.
concepts.attestation_source: Folk-traditional in each culture; the Chinese 不耻下问 is from the Analects.

proverbs.original: 聞くは一時の恥、聞かぬは一生の恥。
proverbs.transliteration: Kiku wa ittoki no haji, kikanu wa isshō no haji.
proverbs.literal_en: Asking is a moment's shame; not asking is a lifetime's shame.
proverbs.meaning_en: Swallow the small embarrassment; avoid the permanent ignorance.
proverbs.notes: The canonical Japanese form of the concept.

proverbs.literal_en: Not ashamed to ask those below.
proverbs.meaning_en: The truly learned ask even their inferiors.
proverbs.notes: From the Analects (5.15), where Confucius praises a minister for exactly this.

proverbs.literal_en: By asking and asking, Baghdad is found.
proverbs.meaning_en: Questions will get you anywhere — even Baghdad.
proverbs.notes: Baghdad as the far, fabled destination of the caravan roads.

proverbs.literal_en: The tongue will lead you to Kyiv.
proverbs.meaning_en: Ask your way and you will arrive.
proverbs.notes: Kyiv as the pilgrimage destination of the East Slavic world — the exact twin of the Turkish Baghdad form.

proverbs.literal_en: The tip of the tongue for a guide.
proverbs.meaning_en: Your tongue — your questions — will guide you.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form; rhymed języka/przewodnika.

proverbs.original: Better to ask the way than go astray.
proverbs.literal_en: Better to ask the way than go astray.
proverbs.meaning_en: A question beats a wrong road.
proverbs.notes: English rhymed form; folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: Asking costs nothing.
proverbs.meaning_en: There is no price on a question.
proverbs.notes: Everyday German form.

concepts.title: The fish rots from the head
concepts.gloss: Corruption starts at the top — leadership decays first.
concepts.attestation_source: Proverbial in Greek and Turkish tradition; recorded in European collections from the 16th century (Erasmus-era).

proverbs.original: Το ψάρι βρωμάει από το κεφάλι.
proverbs.transliteration: To psári vromáei apó to kefáli.
proverbs.literal_en: The fish stinks from the head.
proverbs.meaning_en: Blame for rot lies with the leadership.
proverbs.notes: The standard Greek form — a staple of political talk.

proverbs.literal_en: The fish smells from the head.
proverbs.notes: The standard Turkish form; the Greek and Turkish traditions share this one closely.

proverbs.literal_en: The fish rots from the head.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: The fish rots from the head down.
proverbs.literal_en: The fish rots from the head down.
proverbs.notes: Borrowed into English from the Mediterranean tradition; now standard in political and business speech.

proverbs.literal_en: The fish stinks from the head.
proverbs.notes: Standard Italian form.

proverbs.literal_en: The fish spoils from the head.
proverbs.notes: Standard Polish form.

proverbs.original: Der Fisch stinkt vom Kopf her.
proverbs.literal_en: The fish stinks from the head.
proverbs.notes: Standard German form.

proverbs.transliteration: Shàng liáng bú zhèng xià liáng wāi.
proverbs.literal_en: If the upper beam is not straight, the lower beam is crooked.
proverbs.meaning_en: Subordinates bend to the shape of their superiors.
proverbs.notes: The Chinese swaps the fish for carpentry — the roof-beam metaphor of moral leadership.

concepts.title: The frog at the bottom of the well
concepts.gloss: A narrow world produces a narrow mind — the provincial mistakes their horizon for the whole sky.
concepts.attestation_source: Zhuangzi, 'Autumn Floods' — the frog of the caved-in well cannot be told about the sea.

proverbs.literal_en: The frog at the bottom of the well.
proverbs.meaning_en: One whose world is the well's mouth wide.
proverbs.notes: From Zhuangzi's 'Autumn Floods' dialogue — the source of the whole East Asian family.

proverbs.original: 井の中の蛙大海を知らず。
proverbs.transliteration: I no naka no kawazu taikai o shirazu.
proverbs.literal_en: The frog in the well knows nothing of the great ocean.
proverbs.meaning_en: The sheltered cannot conceive the wider world.
proverbs.notes: The Japanese completes Zhuangzi's image with the unseen ocean.

proverbs.literal_en: The frog inside the well.
proverbs.meaning_en: One who mistakes their small world for the world.
proverbs.notes: Standard Korean form of the shared East Asian image.

proverbs.literal_en: Like a frog under a coconut shell.
proverbs.meaning_en: Living under a small dome and calling it the sky.
proverbs.notes: The Malay/Indonesian frog sits under a coconut half-shell instead of down a well.

proverbs.original: Ếch ngồi đáy giếng coi trời bằng vung.
proverbs.literal_en: The frog sitting at the bottom of the well thinks the sky is the size of a pot-lid.
proverbs.meaning_en: The narrow view mistakes itself for the whole.
proverbs.notes: The Vietnamese frog measures the sky against a kitchen pot-lid.

proverbs.literal_en: Well-frog.
proverbs.notes: A Sanskrit compound in continuous use in Hindi and other Indian languages — the Indic branch of the same ancient image.

concepts.title: Don't put off until tomorrow what you can do today
concepts.gloss: Delay is the thief of the task — do it now.
concepts.attestation_source: Lord Chesterfield's Letters (1749) — 'no idleness, no laziness, no procrastination; never put off till tomorrow what you can do today'; older Latin school maxims behind it.

proverbs.original: Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today.
proverbs.literal_en: Never put off till tomorrow what you can do today.
proverbs.notes: Chesterfield's phrasing (1749), reinforced by Franklin's almanacs.

proverbs.original: No dejes para mañana lo que puedas hacer hoy.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't leave for tomorrow what you can do today.
proverbs.notes: Standard Spanish form.

proverbs.original: Ne remets pas à demain ce que tu peux faire aujourd'hui.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't put back to tomorrow what you can do today.
proverbs.notes: Standard French form.

proverbs.original: Was du heute kannst besorgen, das verschiebe nicht auf morgen.
proverbs.literal_en: What you can take care of today, do not shift to tomorrow.
proverbs.notes: The rhymed besorgen/morgen couplet — memorised by generations of German schoolchildren.

proverbs.original: Не откладывай на завтра то, что можно сделать сегодня.
proverbs.transliteration: Ne otkladyvay na zavtra to, chto mozhno sdelat' segodnya.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't postpone to tomorrow what can be done today.
proverbs.notes: Standard Russian form.

proverbs.original: Não deixes para amanhã o que podes fazer hoje.
proverbs.literal_en: Don't leave for tomorrow what you can do today.
proverbs.notes: Standard Portuguese form.

proverbs.literal_en: Don't leave today's work to tomorrow.
proverbs.notes: Standard Turkish form.

proverbs.literal_en: Today's affairs, finished today.
proverbs.meaning_en: Close each day's work within the day.
proverbs.notes: Standard Chinese form; a school and workplace motto.

concepts.title: When you drink the water, remember the spring
concepts.gloss: Gratitude to those whose earlier work you now enjoy.
concepts.attestation_source: 庾信 Yu Xin, 'Zhi Diao Qu' — origin of the Chinese 饮水思源; the Vietnamese form is folk-traditional.

proverbs.literal_en: Drinking water, think of the source.
proverbs.meaning_en: Remember what — and who — your good fortune flows from.
proverbs.notes: Coined from Yu Xin's 6th-century verse; a fixture of school mottos across the Chinese-speaking world.

proverbs.original: Ăn quả nhớ kẻ trồng cây.
proverbs.literal_en: Eating the fruit, remember the one who planted the tree.
proverbs.meaning_en: Owe your enjoyment to its maker — and remember them.
proverbs.notes: One of the most-taught Vietnamese proverbs; central to the culture of gratitude toward forebears.

proverbs.original: Bir fincan kahvenin kırk yıl hatırı vardır.
proverbs.literal_en: A cup of coffee has forty years of remembrance.
proverbs.meaning_en: Even a small kindness obliges long loyalty.
proverbs.notes: The classic Turkish coffee proverb — hospitality creates a forty-year bond.
